## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{100}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why must a moving machine keep checking its commands when its learned model stops responding?_

A learned model can pause for a fraction of a second while it interprets a scene, but the machine carrying it keeps moving, and a loaded base covers tens of centimeters in that pause. Every delay between a decision and the current it becomes is therefore paid in clearance. A general-purpose computer hides such delays behind queues, retries, and priorities. A moving machine cannot, because a command that arrives late acts on a body that has already moved, and a check that waits on the model it checks protects nothing once that model stalls. Treating timing and communication as implementation details produces machines whose safeguards share a processor, a supply rail, or a memory bus with the model they guard, and so fail together with it. A machine that acts on learned decisions therefore needs a timed path between proposal and actuator whose delays are bounded, whose checks never wait on the proposer, and whose grant of authority to each proposal expires on its own. At the causal boundary, time granted to a proposal becomes motion that software cannot recall.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Explain why the permission path's independence from the proposer is a requirement to be demonstrated rather than a property of separate processors
- Derive suitable update rates from actuator time constants, sampling delay, and learned proposal renewal limits
- Evaluate mailbox exchanges for bounded reads, complete payloads, and proposal freshness when the writer stalls
- Size a chunk lease between the renewal floor and the stopping budget's pre-brake ceiling
- Distinguish measured latency percentiles from response-time bounds that include computation, blocking, and interference
- Compare position, velocity, torque, and impedance commands by what each leaves the permission path to check
- Diagnose interface timing violations by comparing each handoff's allocated budget with like-for-like evidence
- Construct handoff records that state operating conditions, evidence categories, detectors, and bound kinds

:::

## The Multi-Rate Bridge {#sec-nervous-multi-rate-bridge}

Every machine that acts on learned decisions joins two kinds of computation that run on different clocks. A learned model turns camera frames into a proposal in tens to hundreds of milliseconds, and its latency varies from one frame to the next. A motor drive regulates winding current every few tens of microseconds and cannot pause, because the mass it moves does not pause. The layer between them, the machine's **Nervous System**\index{Nervous system!architecture}, carries proposals down toward the actuators and measurements back up, and decides whether each proposal may move the machine at all. Industrial motion control, avionics, and automotive electronics built such layers long ago for classical controllers, whose timing could be analyzed before deployment [@kopetz2011real]. A learned proposer is harder to accommodate. Its latency has a tail, it can stall without warning, and its output can be wrong in ways no one can enumerate in advance.

The central question of this chapter follows from that asymmetry. It is how long one proposal may keep driving the machine when its successor does not arrive, and what must hold in the silicon, the exchange, the bus, and the power supply for that answer to stand. The chapter derives the answer from the machine's physics rather than choosing it as a software timeout. The first requirement is that inference stay off the timed actuator path; @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning states that requirement in the vocabulary of real-time scheduling and adopts a two-processor split as the hypothesis on which the machine is built, a hypothesis that @sec-placement later tests on its silicon. @Sec-nervous-cadences then sets each loop's rate, lets the slow writer publish without ever blocking the fast reader, and sizes the chunk lease that ends a stale proposal's authority; @sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses bounds the time a command takes to reach the drives. The sections that follow restrict actuation privilege to the permission path, define what a proposal may command, contain the proposer's faults, and check each command against physical invariants. The chapter closes Part I with the handoff record, which places five interface limits at each handoff, and with one budget that couples this chapter's lease to the limits of @sec-body and @sec-brain.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_pa.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Plan-Act edge."}

*Proposals cross from Plan to Act only through the permission path.*
:::

The running machine shows the gap concretely. The warehouse mobile manipulator that this book follows regulates the current in its motor windings thousands of times per second, while the learned models that proposed its grasp on the conveyor mug in @sec-brain need orders of magnitude longer to digest each camera frame. If motor regulation waits on deliberative reasoning or on shared resources without a bounded response time, an inference workload can delay the control loop past its deadline. The physics of moving mass and electromagnetic coils create a strict architectural requirement: *the Brain needs time to deliberate, while the Body needs continuous control to survive.*

A shared blocking path makes the faster loop depend on the slower one. If control waits for inference or drains a queue of old setpoints, the command reaches a body that has already moved. Transport delay ($\tau_{\text{transport}}$) also adds phase lag to feedback, a lag of $\Delta\phi = \omega \tau_{\text{transport}}$ radians at angular frequency $\omega$, so a correction arrives later in the motion it was intended to regulate. The Nervous System must bound those delays while keeping local control available when deliberation stalls.

::: {.column-margin}
<!-- fig-alt hand-types the four periods; MachineTiers guards them (500 ms, 50 ms, 1 ms, 50 us).
     Drawn by generate_margin_figures.py (ch04_cadence_tier_ladder); --check fails on drift. -->
![](images/svg/margin_cadence_tier_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Ladder of four horizontal bars on a log time axis, longest at top: intent 500 milliseconds, chunk 50 milliseconds, tick 1 millisecond, current 50 microseconds."}

*Each tier runs at least ten times faster than the one above it, and none may wait on a slower one.*
:::

The Nervous System arranges the machine's computation in four tiers, which separate responsibilities as well as update rates. Faster tiers must continue their checks without waiting for slower ones:

1. **Actuator current and velocity regulation:** The motor drive closes the winding-current loop and the joint velocity loop locally. Field-Oriented Control (FOC)[^fn-foc-motor-drive] coordinates the applied voltage with rotor position to produce the requested torque.
2. **Permission and position supervision:** The permission path checks proposal freshness and physical limits, sends admitted position setpoints to the drives, checks measured motion against them, and requests a feasible fallback when authority expires.
3. **Action-chunk policy:** The learned policy proposes a short sequence of waypoints, allowing local control to proceed between inference results.
4. **Intent planning:** The slower model supplies task goals that guide the chunk policy without directly commanding the drives.

[^fn-foc-motor-drive]: **Field-Oriented Control (FOC)**: The drive rotates the three measured phase currents into a frame that turns with the rotor's magnetic field, where torque and flux become two slowly varying currents that ordinary proportional-integral loops can hold. The rotation needs a fresh rotor angle in every carrier period, so the loop cannot wait on anything slower than its own sensors. That is why the current loop runs inside the drive, beside the encoder and the current shunts, and why no proposer, however fast, ever sits inside it. \index{Field-oriented control!drive current loop}

The rate calculation in @sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag assigns these roles their timing budgets. Enforcement algorithms and joint dynamics are developed in @sec-enforcement; the architectural requirement here is that a stalled proposer cannot suspend the faster checks.

In standard computer systems, workloads share processors, caches, and memory interconnects under general-purpose operating systems. When a neural network streams multi-gigabyte weight tensors across a shared memory bus, its transfers can contend with control traffic, and no thread priority can preempt a hardware transaction already occupying the bus. A control path that waits for that engine can also lose timely setpoint updates during a garbage-collection pause, page fault, or thermal throttle. Local control must remain available without waiting for fresh inference.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-machine-stall-travel
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BASE TRAVEL DURING ONE PROPOSER INFERENCE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-multi-rate-bridge, the running-machine bullets.
# │ Goal:    Show how far the base moves while each learned proposer computes.
# │ Show:    60 mm in one 40 ms chunk inference, 503 mm in one computed
# │          336 ms intent inference, at the 1.5 m/s drive limit.
# │ How:     Distance = drive limit x inference latency, all from the registry.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class MachineStallTravel:
    """Base travel at the drive limit during one inference of each learned proposer."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    t_chunk = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative (P99, incl. vision)
    t_intent = RM.intent_inference_latency  # category: derived (prefill plus decode, @sec-brain-memory-wall)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    d_chunk = (v * t_chunk).to(millimeter)
    d_intent = (v * t_intent).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Drive limit drifted: {v}")
    check(abs(t_chunk.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk inference latency drifted: {t_chunk}")
    # 2026-09-28 (M2): intent latency computed, no longer a stipulated 160 ms.
    check(abs(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude - 335.61) < 5e-3, f"Intent inference latency drifted: {t_intent}")
    check(abs(d_chunk.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-6, f"Chunk-inference travel drifted: {d_chunk}")
    check(abs(d_intent.magnitude - 503.41) < 5e-3, f"Intent-inference travel drifted: {d_intent}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    t_chunk_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_intent_str = fmt_latency(round(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_chunk_str = fmt_length(d_chunk, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_intent_str = fmt_length(round(d_intent.magnitude) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
```

@Sec-brain established how long each learned proposer on the machine needs to turn camera frames into a proposal. An electromagnetic motor coil has an electrical time constant ($\tau_e = L/R$) measured in fractions of a millisecond, while moving linkages carry kinetic energy ($E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$). Delaying or miscalculating the current command can therefore exhaust a physical margin before deliberation finishes. On the mobile manipulator, the mismatch takes two forms:

- The base (Class 1) cruises at up to its `{python} MachineStallTravel.v_str` drive limit (illustrative; see the Reader Guide), so it travels `{python} MachineStallTravel.d_chunk_str` during one `{python} MachineStallTravel.t_chunk_str` chunk-policy inference and `{python} MachineStallTravel.d_intent_str` during one `{python} MachineStallTravel.t_intent_str` intent-model inference, and nothing brakes it in that time unless a process other than the proposer is watching.
- The arm (Class 2) carries reflected rotor inertia ($N^2 J$) through its gearboxes; if its high-rate impedance loops are interrupted while the gripper is on a door latch or a mug, continuing motion can raise the contact force. Whether the force exceeds its limit depends on the measured friction, compliance, and motion response as well as the reflected inertia.

Software discipline, OS thread priorities, and runtime exception handlers cannot by themselves keep the plant safe. Safety requires an explicit, deterministic computing, memory, and communication fabric. That fabric is the Nervous System of the five-level machine (@sec-boundary-machine-model), and it holds the permission path. Each mechanism must leave the physical plant a measured, feasible response when the proposer pauses.

The design requirement at this stage is an interface whose timing, authority, and fault response can be checked against the physical budget. The enforcement algorithms in @sec-enforcement turn that requirement into per-tick decisions; @sec-placement tests whether the chosen hardware preserves it under shared-resource interference. The mechanisms below establish what those later implementations must deliver.

## The Independence Requirement and the Two-Processor Hypothesis {#sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning}

The chunk policy needs enough computation and memory bandwidth to publish proposals at its renewal rate. The permission path needs an upper bound on the time required to check and act on them. These are different requirements. A delayed inference result can be rejected while local control continues; a delayed permission check spends part of the response budget whether or not the processor eventually catches up.

An operating-system scheduler decides which ready task executes next. Raising a control task's priority can reduce competition for the processor, but it cannot make every operation that task performs finish on time. A page fault may suspend the task while memory becomes available; a shared lock may leave it waiting for another task; a memory request may wait behind accelerator transfers already occupying the bus. Inference latency tails[^fn-math-inference-latency] therefore matter even when the average proposal arrives on time.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-tick-vocabulary
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE PERMISSION TICK AS A PERIODIC REAL-TIME TASK (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning, the real-time vocabulary
# │          paragraph; reused by the RTA example in @sec-nervous-rta-variance.
# │ Goal:    Give period, deadline, WCET, and unloaded execution time on the
# │          machine's own tick so each term is defined on a real quantity.
# │ Show:    period 1 ms; deadline 400 us; declared WCET 250 us; unloaded 135 us.
# │ How:     All from AISLE (the same values @sec-placement uses).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class TickVocabulary:
    """The permission tick's period, deadline, and execution-time terms."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_period = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen (1 kHz permission tick)
    t_deadline = AISLE.enforcer_deadline  # category: chosen
    t_wcet = AISLE.enforcer_wcet  # category: chosen (declared)
    t_unloaded = AISLE.enforcer_unloaded  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_wcet_gap = (t_wcet - t_unloaded).to(microsecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_period.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, f"Tick period drifted: {t_period}")
    check(abs(t_deadline.to(microsecond).magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-9, f"Tick deadline drifted: {t_deadline}")
    check(abs(t_wcet.to(microsecond).magnitude - 250.0) < 1e-9, f"Declared WCET drifted: {t_wcet}")
    check(abs(t_unloaded.to(microsecond).magnitude - 135.0) < 1e-9, f"Unloaded execution drifted: {t_unloaded}")
    check(t_unloaded < t_wcet < t_deadline < t_period, "Unloaded < WCET < deadline < period")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_deadline_str = fmt_latency(t_deadline.to(microsecond), unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_wcet_str = fmt_latency(t_wcet.to(microsecond), unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_unloaded_str = fmt_latency(t_unloaded.to(microsecond), unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_wcet_gap_str = fmt_latency(t_wcet_gap, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
```

Timing claims in this chapter use the vocabulary of real-time scheduling [@buttazzo2011hard; @kopetz2011real], and each term can be defined on the permission tick itself. The tick is a periodic task. It is released once every **period**\index{Period (real-time task)} $T$, here `{python} TickVocabulary.t_period_str`, and each release must finish by its relative **deadline**\index{Deadline!relative} $D$, measured from the release and chosen here as `{python} TickVocabulary.t_deadline_str`. A deadline is *hard* when a single miss can cause the failure the system exists to prevent, and the tick's deadline is hard in that sense. The time from release to completion is the job's **response time**\index{Response time} $R$. Part of it is execution, which the job's **worst-case execution time (WCET)**\index{Worst-case execution time}[^fn-wcet-control-tick] $C$ bounds.

[^fn-wcet-control-tick]: **Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET)**: A static WCET is a bound proved over every path through the binary and every state the processor's caches and pipeline can be in; analyzers compute it by abstract interpretation of the code against a model of that hardware [@wilhelm2008worst]. Caches, branch predictors, and shared buses make that model either pessimistic or intractable, so a timed path earns a tight bound by avoiding them, which is why the bounded sources listed in @sec-nervous-rta-variance favor tightly coupled memory and fixed pipelines, giving up average speed for a bound that analysis can prove. \index{Worst-case execution time!static analysis}

::: {#dfn-nervous-worst-case-execution-time .callout-definition title="Worst-case execution time"}

***Worst-case execution time***\index{Worst-case execution time!definition}\index{WCET!definition} is the longest time a task can take to run to completion on a given processor, over every admissible input and every state its caches, pipeline, and buses can be in, with no other task competing for the processor.

1.  **Significance**: It is the $C$ term of every response bound in this chapter, and every margin above it is sized on it. The permission tick declares `{python} TickVocabulary.t_wcet_str` against an unloaded run of `{python} TickVocabulary.t_unloaded_str`, so the `{python} TickVocabulary.t_wcet_gap_str` between them is a claim that analysis must justify before the `{python} TickVocabulary.t_deadline_str` deadline, and the stopping budget behind it, can rely on the number.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a mean or a high percentile such as $P_{99}$, which describe the executions a test happened to reach, the WCET covers every admissible path and processor state. A declared WCET is a third quantity, a number the design commits to, which evidence must show is no smaller than the true one.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Recording the largest measured execution time as the WCET. A measured maximum can refute a declared bound but never establish it, because a test campaign reaches only some of the processor states in which the code can run [@wilhelm2008worst].

:::

The rest of the response is waiting. **Blocking**\index{Blocking time} $B$ is time spent waiting for a lower-priority task to release a resource the job needs, and **interference**\index{Interference (scheduling)} $I$ is time taken by higher-priority tasks and interrupts that preempt it. **Jitter**\index{Jitter} is the variation, from one period to the next, in the instant a periodic event happens. A release, a completion, and a sample each have their own jitter, and a tick released on time can still complete late. @Sec-nervous-rta-variance combines $C$, $B$, and $I$ into a bound on $R$.

@Fig-04-permission-tick lays these terms out on one tick of the running machine. The hatched interval is the part of the declared bound that no stress-free run has exercised; the slack after it is what blocking and interference may consume before the deadline.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-permission-tick-strip
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LEGO VALUES FOR @fig-04-permission-tick
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: caption of @fig-04-permission-tick and its plotting cell.
# │ Goal:    Compute and guard the values the caption prints, before the
# │          figure div, so the caption can reference them.
# │ How:     See the class docstring; every value from RM / AISLE.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class TickPermissionStrip:
    """One permission tick drawn to scale, with travel per tick."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_period = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: datasheet (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    d_tick = (v * t_period).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(d_tick.magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Travel per tick drifted: {d_tick}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_tick_str = fmt_length(d_tick, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, precision=1)
```

::: {#fig-04-permission-tick fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**One permission tick**: A job is released at the start of each `{python} TickPermissionStrip.t_period_str` period and must finish by its `{python} TickVocabulary.t_deadline_str` deadline. The unloaded run of `{python} TickVocabulary.t_unloaded_str` is a measurement; the declared WCET of `{python} TickVocabulary.t_wcet_str` is the bound the schedule assumes, and the hatched `{python} TickVocabulary.t_wcet_gap_str` between them is what WCET analysis must justify. The slack to the deadline is the budget for blocking and interference. The bottom row counts the base's travel on the same axis, `{python} TickPermissionStrip.d_tick_str` per tick at the `{python} TickPermissionStrip.v_str` drive limit." fig-alt="Timing strip over one millisecond. Top row, measured: a bar from 0 to 135 microseconds labeled unloaded run. Second row, declared: a solid bar to 135 microseconds, a hatched bar from 135 to 250 microseconds labeled declared WCET 250 microseconds with 115 microseconds to justify, and a dashed outline from 250 to 400 labeled slack 150 microseconds. Vertical lines mark the release at 0, a red dashed deadline at 400 microseconds, and the next release at 1000 microseconds, under a bracket labeled period 1 ms. A travel row below marks 0 to 1.5 millimeters, 1.5 millimeters per tick at 1.5 meters per second."}

```{python}
#| label: fig-04-permission-tick
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ONE PERMISSION TICK (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-04-permission-tick in @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning.
# │ Goal:    Put period, deadline, declared WCET, and unloaded execution on one
# │          to-scale axis, with the base's travel during the tick beneath it.
# │ Show:    release 0; unloaded 135 us; WCET 250 us; deadline 400 us; next
# │          release 1000 us; 1.5 mm per tick at 1.5 m/s.
# │ How:     mlsysim.viz.permission_tick_strip(AISLE, RM.base.max_velocity);
# │          every duration from AISLE, as in TickVocabulary.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

fig, ax, axd = viz.plot_timing_strip(viz.permission_tick_strip(AISLE, TickPermissionStrip.v))
plt.show()
```
:::

Blocking has one failure that priority alone cannot repair. In **priority inversion**\index{Priority inversion}, a high-priority task waits for a resource held by a low-priority task, and medium-priority tasks, which need nothing from either, preempt the holder and so delay the high-priority task for as long as they keep running. Only the lock protocol can bound that wait. The Mars Pathfinder resets (war story \ref{ws-nervous-1997-mars-pathfinder-priority-inversion}) are the canonical case.

Real-time operating-system mechanisms address particular sources of delay. Preallocating and locking memory avoids demand paging in the timed loop; assigning processor affinity avoids migrations; priority inheritance lets a low-priority lock holder finish when a higher-priority task needs its lock. These mechanisms need configuration and timing evidence. @Sec-appendix-systems-timers develops the scheduling, interrupt, and memory mechanisms needed to calculate their contribution to a response bound.

Shared hardware adds delays that software priority does not control. A control task cannot read an encoder buffer while another device monopolizes the route to that buffer, and the memory, supply, heat path, and clock that two processors share can each delay or silence the permission path without any software fault. The inventory of those couplings, and the evidence that would refute a claim to have cut them, belongs to placement (@sec-placement-two-paths-one-die). The requirement it tests is stated here: the permission path must meet its response bound and keep its authority to refuse under any load the proposer can generate.

Dedicated motor-control hardware shortens the path from sensing to actuation. Local sensor interfaces, timer registers, and on-chip memory keep current regulation independent of the host's inference runtime. The integrated driver in @fig-real-motor-controller illustrates this arrangement at small scale: a current-sense resistor beside the chip provides feedback, and power transistors inside the package switch the motor windings. Hardware timers also enforce the separation between complementary switch transitions needed to avoid a short circuit through the bridge.[^fn-hw-epwm-deadtime]

[^fn-math-inference-latency]: **Inference Latency Distribution**\index{Inference latency}: The median and $P_{99}$ alone do not fix the exceedance probability at a given deadline, which must be measured or modeled separately. Tail-model assumptions and exceedance estimates require representative workload data and an account of dependence and uncertainty; @sec-appendix-ml-evt develops these conditions.

[^fn-hw-epwm-deadtime]: **Dead-Time Delay**\index{Dead-time delay}: Dedicated pulse-width modulation timers insert hardware-enforced dead-time delays ($100\text{--}500\text{ ns}$) between complementary high-side and low-side gate signals. This delay ensures that the conducting power switch fully turns off before its opposing switch conducts, preventing shoot-through short circuits across high-voltage DC rails. Because dead time slightly distorts the applied phase voltage, motor control firmware incorporates online volt-second compensation to maintain smooth torque generation.

::: {#fig-real-motor-controller fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Integrated motor-driver silicon**: A Trinamic TMC2209 stepper-motor driver in a QFN package, with a low-value current-sense resistor (marked R110) beside it on the board. The chip carries its own power transistors and current regulation, so the winding current is measured and switched next to the motor it drives rather than by the host processor. A photograph shows the placement; the timing of the current loop is a property of the silicon that the datasheet and measurement must establish. (Photo: Phiarc, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Trinamic_TMC2209_stepper_motor_controller_chip.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0)." fig-alt="Macro photograph of a square QFN integrated circuit marked TMC2209-LA on a black printed circuit board, with a larger surface-mount resistor marked R110 at upper left and small capacitors and copper traces around it."}
![](images/jpg/fig04_real_motor_drive_controller.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

The machine is built on one answer to that requirement, adopted here as a hypothesis. In the two-processor implementation (@fig-04-two-processor-implementation), deliberative planning and reactive enforcement do not share a processor core, a cache hierarchy, or a common memory bus. The slow, stochastic path runs on parallel hardware (Linux host application processors and tensor accelerators) optimized for raw throughput across wide data streams, while the fast, deterministic path runs on isolated hardware (bare-metal microcontrollers or field-programmable gate array (FPGA) cores) optimized for worst-case execution time and cycle-counted predictability. On the mobile manipulator, the permission path runs on a discrete safety microcontroller (MCU) with its own memory. Proposals reach it as framed packets over a board-level link; no memory is shared between the two processors. Structurally, this establishes a hardware-enforced capability ring: the host machine acts strictly as an unprivileged client with zero memory-mapped input/output (MMIO) access to motor drive registers, while the microcontroller holds exclusive hardware write privilege. Separate chips are one realization; a single die can also host the permission path if its response bound and fault containment are shown to hold. Choosing between them is the placement decision of @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die, and until that chapter's loaded tests are run the split is a design hypothesis, not a demonstrated separation. Scheduling both paths on shared cores is the problem of *mixed-criticality scheduling*\index{Mixed-criticality scheduling!first use}, in which each task carries execution-time bounds of increasing assurance and the scheduler guarantees each deadline only under the bound its own criticality demands, so the proposer may overrun while the permission path may not [@vestal2007preemptive]; @sec-placement-isolation-decisions develops it with the memory-bandwidth regulation that shared memory also needs.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-two-processor-rates
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TWO-PROCESSOR RATES (LEGO GUARD FOR A HAND-DRAWN FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-04-two-processor-implementation (fig04_two_processor.svg).
# │ Goal:    Keep the rates drawn in the SVG equal to the registry values.
# │ Show:    intent model 2 Hz; chunk renewal 20 Hz; permission tick 1 kHz.
# │ How:     Read the registry; check() fails the build if a registry change
# │          leaves the SVG labels stale. Nothing prints.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check

class TwoProcessorRates:
    """Registry rates that fig04_two_processor.svg draws as text."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
    f_intent = RM.intent_rate.to(hertz).magnitude  # category: chosen
    f_chunk = RM.chunk_rate.to(hertz).magnitude  # category: chosen
    f_tick = RM.permission_rate.to(hertz).magnitude  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(f_intent - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"SVG draws the intent model at 2 Hz; registry says {f_intent}.")
    check(abs(f_chunk - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"SVG draws chunk renewal at 20 Hz; registry says {f_chunk}.")
    check(abs(f_tick - 1000.0) < 1e-9, f"SVG draws a 1 kHz permission tick; registry says {f_tick}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    # Guard-only class: it pins the values drawn in the figure; no prose outputs.
```

::: {#fig-04-two-processor-implementation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The two-processor implementation**: The application processor runs the learned proposers and has no access to the drive registers. Proposals cross a black-channel board link as framed packets; the microcontroller's receive DMA writes them into a double buffer in its own memory, so the processors share no memory. The permission tick reads the latest proposal, checks it against measured state, freshness, and the lease, and sends only an admitted command to the drives, which close their own current and velocity loops. Measured state returns to the application processor as telemetry over the same link." fig-alt="Three horizontal tiers. Top, application processor: perception feeds an intent model at 2 hertz, which passes a goal to a chunk policy at 20 hertz renewal. Middle band: a dashed black-channel board link, a serial peripheral interface (SPI) bus or a Controller Area Network with Flexible Data-Rate (CAN FD) bus, framed packets with CRC and sequence number, no shared memory. A dashed proposal arrow runs from the chunk policy through the link into a double buffer with seqlock, filled by receive DMA in MCU-local SRAM, inside the safety MCU. The buffer feeds a permission tick at 1 kilohertz that checks freshness, lease, and limits. Bottom: the tick sends an admitted command to drives with current and velocity loops, which move the physical plant; the plant feeds back to encoders and scanner, which feed the permission tick and send telemetry up through the link to perception."}
![](images/svg/fig04_two_processor.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The name *safety microcontroller*\index{Safety microcontroller!definition} claims more than a separate chip. It names a device developed and assessed under the IEC 61508 functional-safety series, whose safety manual states the integrity it can support and the conditions of use that support depends on [@iec61508-2-2010]. Its hardware is built to detect its own faults: two cores run in lockstep while a comparator flags divergent execution; error-correcting codes protect SRAM and flash; a memory protection unit confines each task; monitors watch the clock and the supply voltages; and built-in self-tests run at start-up and during operation. A watchdog outside the device, on its own oscillator and fed within a time window or by answering a challenge, catches a core that has stopped or runs too fast, and a fault that stops the core's clock cannot also stop it.

None of these features rates the machine. Integrity belongs to a safety function, such as ending a proposal's authority when its lease expires. IEC 61508 grades that function by its safety integrity level\index{Safety integrity level (IEC 61508)}, an integer from 1 to 4 in which each step demands roughly a tenfold lower rate of dangerous failure [@iec61508]. The machinery standard ISO 13849-1 grades it by performance level\index{Performance level (ISO 13849)}, from PL a to PL e [@iso13849part1]. A performance level combines four quantities: the channel architecture, called the Category, which runs from a single channel of well-tried components (Categories B and 1) through a single channel with periodic self-tests (Category 2) to two channels arranged so that no single fault defeats the function (Categories 3 and 4); the reliability of the components, stated as a mean time to dangerous failure; the diagnostic coverage\index{Diagnostic coverage}, the fraction of dangerous failures that the built-in tests detect; and the measures taken against a common-cause failure\index{Common-cause failure}, one cause that disables both channels at once. The microcontroller contributes failure rates and diagnostic coverage to that calculation; the required level follows from the risk the function must reduce.

The machine's architecture makes one trade that such a rating must price. Its permission path carries performance functions, checking proposals and turning admitted waypoints into setpoints, beside the one safety function it is rated for: ending authority and commanding a drive stop when a lease expires or the host heartbeat falls silent. The admission checks themselves carry no rating; the drives' certified stop functions and the safety scanner carry the protective claim for the hazards those checks monitor (@sec-enforcement-certified-functions). Functional-safety practice usually keeps a complex control function out of the rated channel and adds an independent monitoring channel, which is how Categories 3 and 4 obtain their second channel. Drives can supply part of that second channel through integrated safety functions such as safe stop 1 (@sec-enforcement-stop-categories), and @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die examines what lockstep does and does not cover when the permission path shares a die.

The partition must preserve exclusive actuator access and bounded permission checks under the faults assigned to it. Dedicated silicon is one way to meet that obligation; physical separation alone does not establish it, and the rest of this chapter builds on the two-processor hypothesis while carrying its evidence obligation forward to @sec-placement. The exchange now has to connect workloads on different clocks without making the faster reader wait for the slower writer.

## Multi-Rate Cadences {#sec-nervous-cadences}

A motor drive cannot wait for the next camera-based proposal before regulating winding current. Conversely, requiring the learned policy to run at the current-loop rate would spend computation without creating equally frequent observations. Separate cadences let each workload meet its own physical or computational deadline, provided the exchange preserves freshness and never blocks local control.

### Physical time constants and sampling phase lag {#sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag}

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-machine-tiers
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE RUNNING MACHINE'S RATE TIERS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-cadences, the four-tier sentence, the perception
# │          paragraph, and the chunk-policy tier paragraph.
# │ Goal:    Give the machine's own proposer rates and chunk horizon, and the
# │          base's travel during one camera exposure.
# │ Show:    chunk policy 20 Hz (50 ms = 2 x 25 ms setpoints, M5), intent model
# │          2 Hz (500 ms), H = 16; 22.5 mm of base
# │          travel in a 15 ms exposure at the 1.5 m/s drive limit.
# │ How:     Rates and horizon from RM; travel = drive limit x exposure, with
# │          the exposure a scenario input.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_frequency, fmt_int, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class MachineTiers:
    """Proposer rates, chunk horizon, and exposure travel on the running machine."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    f_chunk = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen (chunk-policy renewal rate)
    f_intent = RM.intent_rate  # category: chosen (intent-model rate)
    chunk_horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen (setpoints per chunk)
    chunk_step = RM.chunk_step  # category: chosen (setpoint step)
    f_current = RM.current_loop_rate  # category: chosen (drive current-loop rate)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    t_exp = 15 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (exposure in a 300 lux scene; scenario assumption)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    d_exp = (v * t_exp).to(millimeter)
    t_chunk_period = RM.chunk_period  # renewal period, a whole number of setpoint steps
    n_per_renewal = RM.chunk_schedule["setpoints_per_renewal"]
    t_current = (1 / f_current).to(microsecond)  # current-loop sampling period

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(f_current.to(ureg.kHz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Current-loop rate drifted: {f_current}")
    # margin_cadence_tier_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 500 ms, 50 ms, 1 ms, 50 us.
    check(abs(t_current.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"Current-loop period drifted: {t_current}")
    check(abs(RM.chunk_period.to(millisecond).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Ladder: chunk period drifted")
    check(abs((1 / f_intent).to(millisecond).magnitude - 500.0) < 1e-9, "Ladder: intent period drifted")
    # The ladder caption says each tier runs at least ten times faster than the one above it.
    check(
        f_current >= 10 * RM.permission_rate and RM.permission_rate * RM.chunk_period >= 10 and RM.chunk_period * 10 <= 1 / f_intent,
        "Ladder caption: tier ratio fell below ten",
    )
    check(abs(f_chunk.to(hertz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk rate drifted: {f_chunk}")
    check(abs(f_intent.to(hertz).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Intent rate drifted: {f_intent}")
    check(chunk_horizon == 16, f"Chunk horizon drifted: {chunk_horizon}")
    check(abs(chunk_step.to(millisecond).magnitude - 25.0) < 1e-9, f"Setpoint step drifted: {chunk_step}")
    check(n_per_renewal == 2, f"Setpoints per renewal drifted: {n_per_renewal}")
    check(abs(v.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Drive limit drifted: {v}")
    check(abs(d_exp.magnitude - 22.5) < 1e-9, f"Exposure travel drifted: {d_exp}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    f_chunk_str = fmt_frequency(f_chunk, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    f_intent_str = fmt_frequency(f_intent, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    t_intent_period_str = fmt_latency((1 / f_intent).to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_horizon_str = fmt_int(chunk_horizon)
    chunk_step_str = fmt_latency(chunk_step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_current_str = fmt_frequency(f_current, unit=ureg.kHz, precision=0)
    t_current_str = fmt_latency(t_current, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    n_per_renewal_str = fmt_int(n_per_renewal)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    t_exp_str = fmt_latency(t_exp, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_exp_str = fmt_length(d_exp, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

The mobile manipulator's motor inverters regulate winding current every `{python} MachineTiers.t_current_str` (`{python} MachineTiers.f_current_str`), while its chunk policy requires `{python} MachineStallTravel.t_chunk_str` at P99 to ingest camera frames and generate an action chunk. No single execution cadence serves both the body's continuous electromagnetic dynamics and the computational cost of deep visual inference. An embodied machine therefore operates across four coupled cadences (@fig-04-multirate-cadence-buffer), each dictated by a distinct physical and systems time constant:

1. **Inner Commutation and Current Loop (`{python} MachineTiers.f_current_str`, `{python} MachineTiers.t_current_str` cycle):** The pulse-width modulation (PWM) carrier, chosen for switching loss, current ripple, and acoustic noise, fixes the sampling instants: phase currents are sampled once per carrier period at its midpoint, so a `{python} MachineTiers.f_current_str` carrier gives $T_s =$ `{python} MachineTiers.t_current_str`. The stator winding's electrical time constant ($\tau_e = L/R \approx 0.5\text{ ms}$) sets the plant pole that the current regulator compensates, and the closed-loop current bandwidth is placed well above that pole and a factor of ten or more below the sampling rate [@franklin1998digital]. The loop runs inside the drive's own silicon and commands electromagnetic torque through the drive's current controller (@sec-body).
2. **Permission and Position-Supervision Tick ($1\text{ kHz}$, $1000\,\mu\text{s} \pm 10\,\mu\text{s}$ cycle):** The isolated real-time microcontroller checks proposal integrity, freshness, and physical limits, evaluates the admitted trajectory, sends position setpoints to the drives, and checks measured joint position against them; the drives close the joint velocity and current loops. It requests a state-matched fallback when active authority ends. The trajectory construction in @sec-planning supplies smooth motion between waypoints; @sec-enforcement develops the command checks and response selection.
3. **Action-Chunk Policy Stream (`{python} MachineTiers.f_chunk_str`, `{python} MachineTiers.t_chunk_period_str` cycle):** Bridging observation age and mechanical execution, the local policy emits receding-horizon action chunks ($H =$ `{python} MachineTiers.chunk_horizon_str` waypoints spaced `{python} MachineTiers.chunk_step_str` apart). The machine's chunk policy is a compact visuomotor network of the Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) architecture, which decodes a whole chunk in one pass; iterative diffusion or flow-matching heads are the alternatives @sec-training-decoder-costs prices. It runs on the application processor's accelerator, amortizing memory bandwidth weight-streaming overhead ($f \le B/M$) across physical wall-clock execution time.
4. **Multimodal Intent Planner (`{python} MachineTiers.f_intent_str`, `{python} MachineTiers.t_intent_period_str` cycle):** High-capacity Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models evaluate camera frames, linguistic instructions, and scene affordances to emit strategic task goals and navigation targets.

The two proposer cadences are representative of action-chunking and vision-language-action systems as of 2026 and will move as models and accelerators change. The method that follows, a renewal floor set by supply and a ceiling set by the stopping budget, does not depend on them.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Microsecond interrupt latency requirements build upon the sensor freshness bounds introduced in @sec-body-measurement-freshness.
:::

The current loop's rate follows from the winding alone, and the loop closes inside the drive; @sec-appendix-systems derives the winding's $L/R$. The harder rate question sits one level up, at the joint. There the mechanical time constant and structural stiffness dictate the required closed-loop bandwidth, and a digital loop pays for its sampling, computation, and transport in phase. The crossover frequency is the frequency at which the open-loop gain has unit magnitude; phase margin[^fn-phase-margin-bode] measures how much additional lag it can tolerate there before losing its stability margin.

[^fn-phase-margin-bode]: **Phase Margin**: @bode1945network made gain and phase margin the working measures of how far a feedback amplifier stands from oscillation, the practical reading of the stability criterion of @nyquist1932regeneration. For a reader from machine learning, phase margin behaves like a latency budget with a cliff rather than a slope: a loop keeps its damping while delay stays inside the margin and rings, then oscillates, once delay consumes it. A pure delay $\tau$ spends $\omega_c\tau$ of the margin whatever its cause, so a bus cycle, a compute stage, and a sample-and-hold draw on one shared account. \index{Phase margin!delay budget}

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-tick-delay-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TOTAL-DELAY PHASE BUDGET FOR A LOOP CLOSED THROUGH THE TICK (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag, the delay-budget paragraphs.
# │ Goal:    Show that a 20 Hz joint loop cannot close across the permission
# │          tick and the fieldbus, which is why the drives close it (M1).
# │ Show:    ZOH 3.6 deg + bus 7.2 deg + compute 1.8 deg = 12.6 deg against a
# │          5 deg allowance (0.69 ms of total delay); next-tick output 18.0 deg;
# │          highest crossover at 1 kHz 7.9 Hz; 500 Hz ZOH alone 7.2 deg;
# │          1.5 mm of base travel per millisecond of detection delay.
# │ How:     calc_phase_lag_total (appendix_control total-delay formula);
# │          tick, bus, WCET from AISLE; crossover and allowance chosen.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_multiple, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class TickDelayBudget:
    """Phase erosion of a joint loop closed through the permission tick and the bus."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    f_c = 20.0 * hertz  # category: chosen (illustrative joint-loop crossover)
    phi_allow = 5.0 * ureg.degree  # category: chosen (illustrative erosion allowance)
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen (1 kHz permission tick)
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative (EtherCAT cycle)
    t_comp = AISLE.enforcer_wcet  # category: chosen (declared enforcer WCET)
    t_tick_slow = 2.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (500 Hz comparison)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    same_tick = calc_phase_lag_total(f_c, t_tick, compute_delay=t_comp, transport_delay=t_bus, phase_allowance=phi_allow)
    next_tick = calc_phase_lag_total(f_c, t_tick, compute_delay=t_tick, transport_delay=t_bus, phase_allowance=phi_allow)
    slow_zoh = calc_phase_lag_total(f_c, t_tick_slow)
    phi_zoh = same_tick["phase_zoh"].to(ureg.degree).magnitude
    phi_bus = same_tick["phase_transport"].to(ureg.degree).magnitude
    phi_comp = same_tick["phase_compute"].to(ureg.degree).magnitude
    phi_total = same_tick["phase_total"].to(ureg.degree).magnitude
    phi_next = next_tick["phase_total"].to(ureg.degree).magnitude
    phi_slow = slow_zoh["phase_zoh"].to(ureg.degree).magnitude
    tau_total = same_tick["tau_total"].to(millisecond)
    tau_next = next_tick["tau_total"].to(millisecond)
    tau_allowed = same_tick["tau_allowed"].to(millisecond)
    f_max = same_tick["f_crossover_max"].to(hertz)
    over_ratio = phi_total / phi_allow.magnitude
    mm_per_ms = (v * (1 * millisecond)).to(millimeter)
    n_fir = 9  # category: illustrative (moving-average taps, fn-fir-smoothing)
    tau_fir = ((n_fir - 1) / 2 * t_tick).to(millisecond)  # FIR group delay, (N-1)/2 samples
    phi_fir = (360.0 * f_c * tau_fir).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude  # degrees at crossover

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(tau_fir.magnitude - 4.0) < 1e-9, f"FIR group delay drifted: {tau_fir}")
    check(abs(phi_fir - 28.8) < 1e-9, f"FIR phase at crossover drifted: {phi_fir}")
    # margin_tick_phase_budget_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 20 Hz, 5, 3.6, 1.8, 7.2, 12.6 degrees (guarded here).
    check(abs(phi_zoh - 3.6) < 1e-9, f"ZOH phase drifted: {phi_zoh}")
    check(abs(phi_bus - 7.2) < 1e-9, f"Bus phase drifted: {phi_bus}")
    check(abs(phi_comp - 1.8) < 1e-9, f"Compute phase drifted: {phi_comp}")
    check(abs(phi_total - 12.6) < 1e-9, f"Total phase drifted: {phi_total}")
    check(abs(phi_next - 18.0) < 1e-9, f"Next-tick total phase drifted: {phi_next}")
    check(abs(phi_slow - 7.2) < 1e-9, f"500 Hz ZOH phase drifted: {phi_slow}")
    check(phi_zoh < phi_allow.magnitude < phi_bus, "ZOH alone fits the allowance; the bus alone does not")
    check(t_bus > tau_allowed, "The bus cycle alone exceeds the whole delay allowance")
    check(abs(f_max.magnitude - 7.9365) < 1e-3, f"Highest supported crossover drifted: {f_max}")
    check(abs(mm_per_ms.magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Travel per millisecond drifted: {mm_per_ms}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    f_c_str = fmt_frequency(f_c, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    phi_allow_str = fmt(phi_allow.magnitude, precision=0)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_bus_str = fmt_latency(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_comp_str = fmt_latency(t_comp.to(microsecond), unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    phi_zoh_str = fmt(phi_zoh, precision=1)
    phi_bus_str = fmt(phi_bus, precision=1)
    phi_comp_str = fmt(phi_comp, precision=1)
    phi_total_str = fmt(phi_total, precision=1)
    phi_next_str = fmt(phi_next, precision=0)
    phi_slow_str = fmt(phi_slow, precision=1)
    tau_total_str = fmt_latency(tau_total, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    tau_next_str = fmt_latency(tau_next, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    tau_allowed_str = fmt_latency(tau_allowed, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    f_max_str = fmt_frequency(f_max, unit=hertz, precision=1)
    over_mult_str = fmt_multiple(over_ratio, precision=1)
    mm_per_ms_str = fmt_length(mm_per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    n_fir_str = fmt(n_fir, precision=0)
    tau_fir_str = fmt_latency(tau_fir, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    phi_fir_str = fmt(phi_fir, precision=1)
    fir_over_mult_str = fmt_multiple(phi_fir / phi_allow.magnitude, precision=1)
```

Phase lag matters because it makes corrective torques arrive out of phase with the link's motion; enough of it turns stabilizing negative feedback into amplification [@nyquist1932regeneration]. A loop that closes through the permission tick pays three delays, not one. The sample-and-hold acts like half a sample period of pure delay; the controller then needs time between sampling and output; and the command reaches the drive only after the bus carries it. A pure delay $T_d$ removes $\omega T_d$ of phase at every frequency, so near crossover the three together erode the phase margin by the amount in @eq-nervous-delay-phase (@sec-appendix-control-zoh):
$$\Delta\phi = \omega_c\left(\frac{T_s}{2} + \tau_{\text{comp}} + \tau_{\text{bus}}\right)$$ {#eq-nervous-delay-phase}
Take an assumed joint-loop crossover of `{python} TickDelayBudget.f_c_str` and an erosion allowance of `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_allow_str`$^\circ$, both chosen for illustration. A `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_tick_str` tick's sample-and-hold costs `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_zoh_str`$^\circ$, which fits. The `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_bus_str` bus cycle that carries the command costs `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_bus_str`$^\circ$ by itself, and the enforcer's declared `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_comp_str` worst-case execution time adds `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_comp_str`$^\circ$. The total, `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_total_str`$^\circ$ over `{python} TickDelayBudget.tau_total_str` of delay, is `{python} TickDelayBudget.over_mult_str` the allowance, and a controller that holds its output until the next tick reaches `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_next_str`$^\circ$ over `{python} TickDelayBudget.tau_next_str`. The allowance admits only `{python} TickDelayBudget.tau_allowed_str` of total delay, less than the bus cycle alone, so no tick rate can close a `{python} TickDelayBudget.f_c_str` loop across this bus. With a `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_tick_str` tick, the delay supports a crossover of at most `{python} TickDelayBudget.f_max_str`. Halving the tick rate to $500\text{ Hz}$ would raise the sample-and-hold term alone to `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_slow_str`$^\circ$, and raising the rate cannot remove the bus term. The placement of the loop, not the tick rate, resolves the budget.

::: {.column-margin}
<!-- fig-alt hand-types the phase terms; TickDelayBudget guards them (3.6, 1.8, 7.2, 12.6 against 5 degrees).
     Drawn by generate_margin_figures.py (ch04_phase_budget_envelope); --check fails on drift. -->
![](images/svg/margin_tick_phase_budget_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="One stacked horizontal bar of phase lag at a 20 hertz crossover: hold 3.6 degrees, compute 1.8 degrees, and bus 7.2 degrees, totaling 12.6 degrees. A dashed red line at 5 degrees allowed falls inside the compute segment, and the whole bus segment lies in the shaded region past it."}

*The bus cycle alone spends more phase than the loop can spare.*
:::

The machine therefore closes its joint velocity and current loops inside the drives, which sample their own encoders with no bus in the loop, and the permission tick sends position setpoints and supervises the motion they produce. The `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_tick_str` tick must then meet two requirements that are not phase margins. As a supervisor, every millisecond of detection delay costs `{python} TickDelayBudget.mm_per_ms_str` of base travel at the drive limit, a price the stopping budget pays (\ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}). As a setpoint source, it must sample the admitted trajectory finely enough that the drive's own loop receives a smooth reference. Bus delay on that reference path adds tracking lag; it does not erode the drive loop's margin. Any correction the microcontroller does close across the bus, such as an outer position trim, must keep its crossover below `{python} TickDelayBudget.f_max_str`.

Perception, which feeds the chunk policy, executes at an intermediate rate dictated by photon collection physics, exposure windows, and target velocity relative to the sensor field of view. In an illustrative $300\text{ lux}$ scene with a `{python} MachineTiers.t_exp_str` exposure, the base at its `{python} MachineTiers.v_str` drive limit travels $\Delta x = v\,T_{\text{exp}} =$ `{python} MachineTiers.d_exp_str` during the exposure; image-plane blur additionally depends on depth, optics, and camera motion. Exposure signal-to-noise, this displacement, and processing time jointly bound a useful perception rate for the task.

The chunk-policy rate must fit the proposal-supply budget established in @sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline. On the mobile manipulator, a `{python} MachineTiers.f_chunk_str` renewal and a `{python} MachineTiers.chunk_horizon_str`-waypoint chunk, the chunk horizon $H$ of action-chunking policies [@zhao2023learning], bridge observation and actuation rates. The `{python} MachineTiers.t_chunk_period_str` renewal period spans exactly `{python} MachineTiers.n_per_renewal_str` setpoint steps of `{python} MachineTiers.chunk_step_str`, so every renewal begins on a setpoint boundary.

### Lock-free and wait-free mailbox exchanges {#sec-nervous-mailbox-exchanges}

Because these cadences execute on isolated hardware domains at different frequencies, data exchange across rate boundaries must give the timed reader bounded, nonblocking access (@fig-04-multirate-cadence-buffer). If a $1\text{ kHz}$ control loop waits on a mutex lock held by a $20\text{ Hz}$ neural network runtime, a single scheduling delay in the operating system immediately causes priority inversion, forcing the real-time controller to miss its execution deadline.

A communication library does not by itself establish this property. Serialization, memory allocation, queues, and task scheduling can all delay delivery. Shared memory avoids some copying and kernel work, but it still needs a rule that prevents the reader from using a half-written proposal. The contract must bound the reader's work even when the writer stops at the worst possible point.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-multirate-stall
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LEGO VALUES FOR @fig-04-multirate-cadence-buffer
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: caption of @fig-04-multirate-cadence-buffer and its plotting cell.
# │ Goal:    Compute and guard the values the caption prints, before the
# │          figure div, so the caption can reference them.
# │ How:     See the class docstring; every value from RM / AISLE.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, check
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class MultirateStall:
    """One proposer stall on the running machine's clocks, drawn to scale."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_renew = RM.chunk_period.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (M5)
    t_infer = RM.chunk_inference_latency.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative (P99)
    t_step = RM.chunk_step.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (M5)
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus.to(millisecond)  # category: derived (fieldbus cycle)
    t_onset = AISLE.t_brake_onset.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Renewals begin at 0, T, 2T; the third never completes (the stall).
    t_last_adm = t_renew + t_infer  # last admission
    t_expiry = t_last_adm + t_lease  # lease lapses
    t_brake = t_expiry + t_tick + t_bus + t_onset
    renewal_to_onset = (t_brake - t_last_adm).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_last_adm.magnitude - 90.0) < 1e-9, f"Last admission drifted: {t_last_adm}")
    check(abs(t_expiry.magnitude - 150.0) < 1e-9, f"Lease expiry drifted: {t_expiry}")
    check(abs(renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, f"Renewal-to-onset drifted: {renewal_to_onset}")
    check(t_renew + (t_renew - t_infer) / 2 < t_lease, "The lease must outlast one renewal period")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_renew_str = fmt_latency(t_renew, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_infer_str = fmt_latency(t_infer, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_step_str = fmt_latency(t_step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
```

::: {#fig-04-multirate-cadence-buffer fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Multi-rate cadence and the mailbox exchange**: (a) The running machine's clocks during a proposer stall, to scale. The chunk policy renews every `{python} MultirateStall.t_renew_str` and needs `{python} MultirateStall.t_infer_str`; the admitted chunk supplies a setpoint every `{python} MultirateStall.t_step_str`. When the third renewal never completes, the tick keeps executing the admitted chunk only until the `{python} MultirateStall.t_lease_str` lease from the last admission lapses; the tick, bus, and brake onset then put the fallback stop `{python} MultirateStall.renewal_to_onset_str` after that admission. (b) The single-slot seqlock in the microcontroller's own memory, in event order. The receive interrupt makes the counter odd, copies a checked frame, and makes it even; the tick accepts a copy only when it reads the same even value before and after. A tick that preempts a write reads an odd value and keeps its last validated chunk, and a stalled application processor leaves the slot unchanged while the lease runs." fig-alt="Two panels. Panel a, a timeline from 0 to about 210 milliseconds with five lanes. Chunk policy: inference bars from 0 to 40 and 50 to 90, then a hatched stalled bar from 100 onward. Setpoints: ticks every 25 milliseconds from 40 to 140. Lease: a dashed outline from 40 to 100 and a filled bar from 90 to 150 labeled lease 60 ms from last admission. Permission tick: fine lines every 1 millisecond. Drives: tracking until 150, a short green interval to 172 labeled tick plus bus plus onset 22 ms, then a red fallback stop. Dashed vertical lines mark last admission at 90, lease expiry at 150, and a red brake onset at 172. Panel b, three lanes in event order: receive ISR writer, sequence counter, and permission tick reader, in three cases. Clean exchange: the writer copies a frame while the counter goes 7 then 8, and the reader reads 8 twice and accepts. Tick preempts a write: the counter reads 9 during a paused write, the reader rejects, then after the counter becomes 10 the reader accepts. Application processor stalls: no frame arrives and the reader reads 10 again twice."}
