:::

A baseline nonblocking exchange uses a **single-producer single-consumer (SPSC) seqlock mailbox**\index{Sequence lock}[^fn-seqlock-versioned-read] in the microcontroller's own static memory. On the machine's separate chips, the proposal first crosses the board-level link as a framed packet. The microcontroller's link receiver, a direct memory access (DMA) transfer completed by a receive interrupt outside the tick, checks the frame's CRC and sequence number and writes the proposal into the mailbox. The writer is therefore the receive interrupt and the reader is the permission tick, both on the microcontroller; the application processor never touches the mailbox (@sec-placement-boundary-contract).

[^fn-seqlock-versioned-read]: **Versioned Read**: @lamport1977concurrent showed that a reader can detect a write that overlapped its copy without taking any lock. The writer updates a version number before and after the data, the reader reads the two in the opposite order, and a mismatch marks the copy as torn. The construction suits a reader that must never wait, such as the permission tick, because the reader pays for a collision with one discarded copy and never delays the writer. \index{Sequence lock!Lamport versioned read}

The writer, the microcontroller's receive interrupt, makes the counter odd, copies a proposal whose frame has passed its CRC and sequence checks into the slot, and then makes the counter even with release ordering. The reader, the permission path, makes one bounded copy attempt per tick. It rejects the attempt if the counter was odd or changed during the copy, and otherwise promotes the copy to its active spline only after integrity, freshness, and physical-admissibility checks pass, so a rejected read leaves the active spline unchanged and the reader never waits for the writer. Because the tick outranks the receive interrupt, it can preempt a write in progress; the reader then sees the odd counter, drops that snapshot in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ time without spinning, keeps its last validated spline only while its own state, evidence, and lease remain admissible, and initiates the state-matched fallback when that authority ends. A stalled application processor cannot leave the counter odd, because it never writes the mailbox. It simply stops sending frames, and the lease ends the active chunk's authority.

Stated as a test on the two counter reads\index{Sequence lock!shared memory}, the reader accepts a copy only when
$$c_{\text{start}} \equiv c_{\text{end}} \equiv 0 \pmod 2 \quad \text{and} \quad c_{\text{start}} = c_{\text{end}},$$
because an odd value means a write is in progress and a changed value means one began during the copy. Unlike a mutex or a semaphore, the exchange never suspends either side, and the reader never retries within a tick, so its work is $\mathcal{O}(1)$ whatever the writer does. The test holds only if the processor performs the loads in the order written. Between an interrupt writer and the tick on one core, compiler ordering suffices; where a DMA engine or a second core also writes the slot, a data memory barrier is needed, which Arm M-profile cores provide only as the full-system `DMB` [@arm2012an321]. Without it, loads of the payload can be reordered ahead of the counter check, and a torn copy can pass.

A first-in, first-out queue preserves publication order, but that is not always the right contract for motion. If the consumer falls behind, queued proposals describe progressively older physical states. **Backpressure cannot pause moving physical mass**. The reader needs the latest complete admissible proposal and a deadline for using it. This does not forbid buffering the waypoints of an admitted trajectory; those waypoints have a defined execution schedule and remain subject to the proposal's lease. It forbids treating eventual delivery of historical proposals as evidence of timely control. Real-time systems practice names the two contracts. An *event message*\index{Event message} is queued and consumed exactly once, so losing one loses information; a *state message*\index{State message} is updated in place and read without being consumed, so a reader always sees the latest value and a missed update is overwritten by the next [@kopetz2011real]. The proposal mailbox carries state messages, and the single-slot seqlock is a form of Kopetz and Reisinger's non-blocking write protocol, in which the reader detects an overlapping write and never delays the writer [@kopetz1993nbw].

A **wait-free three-slot mailbox**[^fn-wait-free-mailbox] can avoid read/write collisions by assigning separate slots to the writer, the published proposal, and the reader. Atomic publication transfers slot ownership; it must never let the writer overwrite the reader's active slot. Unlike the one-attempt seqlock, this design can provide a complete published snapshot without discarding a collided read. Its extra storage and ownership protocol must still be checked on the target hardware. Simpson's four-slot mechanism reaches the same guarantee, a complete snapshot for a reader that never waits, using only single-bit control variables written with ordinary stores and no atomic read-modify-write instruction [@simpson1990four]. Neither design makes an old proposal fresh or extends its lease.

[^fn-wait-free-mailbox]: **Wait-Free**: @herlihy1991waitfree defined an implementation as wait-free when every operation finishes in a bounded number of its own steps, whatever the other processes do. That is stronger than lock-free progress, which guarantees only that some operation completes while a particular one may retry indefinitely. The one-attempt seqlock read is bounded but can come back empty-handed; the slot mailbox is bounded and always returns a complete snapshot, and the extra slot is the price of that second property. \index{Wait-free synchronization!slot mailbox}

Sequential telemetry has a different requirement. A single-producer single-consumer ring buffer preserves a sequence of records until its bounded capacity fills, whereas the proposal mailbox exposes the latest complete candidate. @Sec-appendix-systems-ipc supplies the shared-memory, slot-ownership, and ring-buffer mechanisms, including memory ordering and cache-line separation. The permission interface needs their bounded access and publication guarantees; it does not need a queue of historical motion commands.

Robotics middleware exposes the same choices as configuration, and its defaults do not make them for the permission path. ROS 2 carries messages over the Data Distribution Service (DDS) or a comparable transport [@macenski2022robot], and its quality-of-service settings map onto the contracts above only in part [@omg2015dds]. A *keep-last* history of depth one gives a subscriber the freshest value, the state-message contract. *Best-effort* reliability drops a lost sample instead of retransmitting it, whereas *reliable* delivery can leave a reader draining a backlog after an outage. A *deadline* setting raises an event when a period passes without a new sample, so it detects lateness in the way a heartbeat does and revokes nothing. A *lifespan* setting discards a sample once its source timestamp plus a configured duration has passed. That expiry depends on synchronized clocks, falls back to reception time when the service detects that they are not, and governs only the delivery of samples, not authority a consumer has already granted. None of the four is a lease, because none is derived from a stopping budget or enforced on the consumer's clock at the point of actuation. Timing also depends on how the middleware schedules callbacks. A ROS 2 executor dispatches ready callbacks under its own policy, and a response bound for a chain of callbacks needs an analysis of that policy together with the processor's scheduler [@casini2019response]. At the control boundary, the controllers of the ros2_control framework read incoming commands through a real-time buffer that makes a single try-lock attempt; when the writer holds the lock, the read fails and the controller keeps its previous command [@rostools2025realtime], the one-attempt read of the seqlock in library form. Whatever the middleware, the permission path still needs its own freshness check and lease. @Sec-memory-failure-modes shows the matching failure on the payload side, a middleware that reports healthy delivery of stale content.

Because the receive interrupt's write is short and resumes as soon as the tick finishes, a collision discards one read attempt without delaying the tick. A link that stops delivering instead leaves the slot unchanged across many ticks, so bounded reader work does not imply bounded publication delay. Something must limit how long the last admitted chunk keeps driving the machine, and that limit is a question about the plant, not the mailbox. Under the irreversibility law (principle \ref{pri-vol4-irreversibility}), each millisecond a stalled proposal keeps its authority is travel that no later check can recall, so the limit must be paid for out of the stopping budget.

### Chunk lease sizing from the stopping budget {#sec-nervous-lease-sizing}

A learned policy can stall for many reasons, among them a page fault, a thermal throttle on the vision accelerator, memory fragmentation, or an unhandled exception in the perception pipeline. The machine does not freeze when it does. The loaded base carries its momentum ($p = mv$), and the permission path keeps turning the last admitted chunk into setpoints. To keep an unrenewed proposal from driving the machine blindly into an obstacle, the permission path must end that proposal's authority on its own clock, without waiting for the proposer to report that it has failed.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-machine-lease-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHUNK LEASE AGAINST THE STOPPING BUDGET (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease, the three-timer paragraph,
# │          the overrun paragraph, @sec-nervous-hardware-isolation,
# │          the H4 paragraph, and the summary takeaways.
# │ Goal:    Add the lease path (stopping-budget row 4) to the running total
# │          that @sec-body-kinetic-momentum left, and state the pre-brake
# │          ceiling the lease must fit inside.
# │ Show:    ceiling 258.3 ms; row 4 = 93.0 mm; running total 742.5 -> 835.5 mm;
# │          renewal-to-onset 82 ms; 176.3 ms of ceiling left; renewal
# │          floor 50 + 5 = 55 ms below the 60 ms lease.
# │ How:     calc_watchdog_lease_bound on D_clear less the fixed overheads;
# │          every term from RM / AISLE (canon §3.2-§3.4).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, fmt_display_math, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class MachineLeaseBudget:
    """Chunk lease sized from the mobile manipulator's stopping budget at its drive limit."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (loaded, dry floor)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end clear distance)
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen (1 kHz permission loop)
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative (EtherCAT cycle)
    f_heartbeat = AISLE.heartbeat_rate  # category: chosen
    t_heartbeat_timeout = AISLE.heartbeat_timeout  # category: chosen
    t_self_watchdog = AISLE.mcu_self_watchdog  # category: chosen
    f_chunk = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen (chunk-policy renewal rate)
    t_renewal_jitter = 5 * millisecond  # category: chosen (renewal-jitter allowance; scenario assumption)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    overhead = (delta_loc + delta_margin).to(millimeter)
    ceiling = calc_watchdog_lease_bound(
        clearance_distance=d_clear - delta_loc - delta_margin,
        initial_velocity=v,
        max_deceleration=a_brake,
    )
    d_brake = ceiling["d_brake"].to(millimeter)
    t_ceiling = ceiling["t_total_delay_max"].to(millisecond)  # whole pre-brake delay, onset included
    d_onset = (v * t_act).to(millimeter)
    prior_total = (d_brake + overhead + d_onset).to(millimeter)  # rows 1-3 (@sec-body-kinetic-momentum)
    t_lease_path = (t_lease + t_tick + t_bus).to(millisecond)
    d_lease_path = (v * t_lease_path).to(millimeter)  # row 4
    running_total = (prior_total + d_lease_path).to(millimeter)
    remaining = (d_clear - running_total).to(millimeter)
    t_renewal_to_onset = (t_lease_path + t_act).to(millisecond)
    t_ceiling_left = (t_ceiling - t_renewal_to_onset).to(millisecond)
    mm_per_ms = (v * (1 * millisecond)).to(millimeter)
    t_chunk_period = (1 / f_chunk).to(millisecond)
    t_renewal_need = (t_chunk_period + t_renewal_jitter).to(millisecond)  # lease lower limit

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_ceiling.magnitude - 258.333) < 5e-3, f"Pre-brake ceiling drifted: {t_ceiling}")
    check(abs(d_brake.magnitude - 562.5) < 1e-6, f"Braking row drifted: {d_brake}")
    check(abs(prior_total.magnitude - 742.5) < 1e-6, f"Rows 1-3 total drifted: {prior_total}")
    check(abs(t_lease_path.magnitude - 62.0) < 1e-6, f"Lease path drifted: {t_lease_path}")
    check(abs(d_lease_path.magnitude - 93.0) < 1e-6, f"Row 4 drifted: {d_lease_path}")
    check(abs(running_total.magnitude - 835.5) < 1e-6, f"Running total drifted: {running_total}")
    check(abs(remaining.magnitude - 264.5) < 1e-6, f"Remaining clear distance drifted: {remaining}")
    check(abs(t_renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-6, f"Renewal-to-onset drifted: {t_renewal_to_onset}")
    check(
        abs((remaining / v).to(millisecond).magnitude - t_ceiling_left.magnitude) < 1e-6,
        "Time left in the ceiling must equal the remaining distance at the drive limit",
    )
    check(abs(t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk lease drifted: {t_lease}")
    check(abs(f_heartbeat.to(hertz).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, f"Heartbeat rate drifted: {f_heartbeat}")
    check(abs(t_heartbeat_timeout.to(millisecond).magnitude - 30.0) < 1e-9, f"Heartbeat timeout drifted: {t_heartbeat_timeout}")
    check(abs(t_self_watchdog.to(millisecond).magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, f"Self-watchdog timeout drifted: {t_self_watchdog}")
    check(abs(t_chunk_period.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-6, f"Chunk period drifted: {t_chunk_period}")
    check(abs(t_renewal_need.magnitude - 55.0) < 1e-6, f"Lease lower limit drifted: {t_renewal_need}")
    check(t_renewal_need < t_lease, "Lease rule: chunk period plus jitter must be shorter than the lease")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    d_onset_str = fmt_length(d_onset, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    prior_total_str = fmt_length(prior_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_ceiling_str = fmt_latency(t_ceiling, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_act_str = fmt_latency(t_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_bus_str = fmt_latency(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_lease_path_str = fmt_length(d_lease_path, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    running_total_str = fmt_length(running_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_ceiling_left_str = fmt_latency(t_ceiling_left, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    mm_per_ms_str = fmt_length(mm_per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    f_heartbeat_str = fmt_frequency(f_heartbeat, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    t_heartbeat_timeout_str = fmt_latency(t_heartbeat_timeout, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_self_watchdog_str = fmt_latency(t_self_watchdog, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_jitter_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_jitter, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_need_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_need, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_margin_str = fmt_length(delta_margin, unit=millimeter, precision=0)

    _v = fmt(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    _a = fmt(a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    _clear = fmt(d_clear, unit=millimeter, precision=0, commas=False)
    _over = fmt(overhead, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    _brake = fmt(d_brake, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _ceil = fmt(t_ceiling, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    _lease = fmt(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _tick = fmt(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _bus = fmt(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _act = fmt(t_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _path = fmt(t_lease_path, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _row4 = fmt(d_lease_path, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    _prior = fmt(prior_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _run = fmt(running_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _rem = fmt(remaining, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _onset = fmt(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _left = fmt(t_ceiling_left, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    _period = fmt(t_chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _jit = fmt(t_renewal_jitter, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _need = fmt(t_renewal_need, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    brake_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\frac{{v^2}}{{2a_{{\text{{brake}}}}}} = \frac{{({_v}\ \text{{m/s}})^2}}{{2 \times {_a}\ \text{{m/s}}^2}} = {_brake}\ \text{{mm}}"
    )
    ceiling_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\tau_{{\text{{delay}}}} \le \frac{{{_clear} - {_over} - {_brake}\ \text{{mm}}}}{{{_v}\ \text{{m/s}}}} = {_ceil}\ \text{{ms}}"
    )
    row4_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"v\,(T_{{\text{{lease}}}} + T_{{\text{{tick}}}} + T_{{\text{{bus}}}}) = {_v}\ \text{{m/s}} \times ({_lease} + {_tick} + {_bus})\ \text{{ms}} = {_row4}\ \text{{mm}}"
    )
    total_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"{_prior} + {_row4} = {_run}\ \text{{mm}}, \quad {_clear} - {_run} = {_rem}\ \text{{mm}}"
    )
    time_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"{_path} + {_act} = {_onset}\ \text{{ms}}, \quad {_ceil} - {_onset} = {_left}\ \text{{ms}}"
    )
    floor_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"T_{{\text{{chunk}}}} + T_{{\text{{jitter}}}} = {_period} + {_jit} = {_need}\ \text{{ms}} < T_{{\text{{lease}}}} = {_lease}\ \text{{ms}}"
    )
```

::: {#dfn-nervous-chunk-lease .callout-definition title="Chunk lease"}

***Chunk lease***\index{Chunk lease!definition}\index{Lease!stopping budget} is the interval, counted on the permission path's own clock from a chunk's admission, during which that admitted chunk may keep driving the actuators without a successful replacement; when it expires, the permission path ends the chunk's authority and commands the state-matched fallback.

1.  **Significance**: The lease enters the pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ of the stopping budget, so each millisecond of it costs $v$ of clear distance, `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.mm_per_ms_str` at the running machine's drive limit. The machine's `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str` lease, with the tick and bus cycle that detect and deliver its expiry, adds `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.d_lease_path_str` to the stopping budget.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a heartbeat timeout, which shows only that the host is alive, a lease is renewed only by a freshly admitted proposal, and its length is derived from the plant rather than configured: above the proposer's renewal floor and below the stopping budget's ceiling. Unlike an evidence deadline, it bounds how long one motion segment may execute, not how long the observation behind it stays valid.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Lengthening the lease to ride out proposer hiccups. A longer lease buys continuity with clearance, and a lease that reaches the pre-brake ceiling commits the machine to motion it can no longer stop in time.

:::

A chunk lease therefore cannot be chosen as a software convenience, such as a round-number heartbeat timeout. In distributed systems, a lease grants time-limited access to a shared resource, such as a cached file, and expires on its own if the holder fails [@gray1989leases]; in physical AI, the resource is motion of a loaded machine. Because the motion cannot be rolled back, the lease duration must come from the stopping budget. The distance traveled during the lease, the detection and transport intervals, and brake onset, plus the braking distance itself, must fit within the clear distance $D_{\text{clear}}$ that remains after localization and protective margins. Rearranging the stopping distance of @eq-body-stopping-distance, $v\,\tau_{\text{delay}} + v^2/2a_{\text{brake}} + \delta_{\text{loc}} + \delta_{\text{margin}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$, and dividing the distance left for travel before braking by the speed gives the **pre-brake ceiling**\index{Pre-brake ceiling}, the longest total delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ that may elapse before braking force begins:
$$\tau_{\text{delay}} \le \frac{D_{\text{clear}} - \delta_{\text{loc}} - \delta_{\text{margin}} - v^2/2a_{\text{brake}}}{v}$$ {#eq-nervous-prebrake}
where $v$ is the speed, $a_{\text{brake}}$ the credible braking deceleration, and $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ and $\delta_{\text{margin}}$ the localization error and protective clearance of @sec-body-kinetic-momentum. As $v$ falls, the braking term shrinks quadratically while the divisor shrinks linearly, so the ceiling grows without limit near rest; at speed, every term the lease path adds to $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ costs $v$ per unit time.

Notebook \ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease} evaluates @eq-nervous-prebrake for the mobile manipulator at its drive limit and prices the lease inside it.

::: {#nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease .callout-notebook title="The price of a lease"}

**Problem**: In the illustrative aisle scenario, the warehouse mobile manipulator cruises at its drive limit toward a person who has stepped out from a rack end and stopped. The permission path admits one last chunk and then receives no admissible replacement. How much time remains before braking must begin, and how much of it, and of the clear distance, does the chunk lease spend?

**Variables**:

* Speed $v =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.v_str`, the drive limit (illustrative); braking deceleration $a_{\text{brake}} =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.a_brake_str`, loaded on a dry floor (illustrative).
* Clear distance $D_{\text{clear}} =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.d_clear_str` (illustrative), less localization error $\delta_{\text{loc}} =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.delta_loc_str` (illustrative) and protective clearance $\delta_{\text{margin}} =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.delta_margin_str` (chosen).
* Brake onset $T_{\text{act}} =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_act_str` (illustrative); permission tick $T_{\text{tick}} =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_tick_str` (chosen); bus cycle $T_{\text{bus}} =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_bus_str` (illustrative).
* Chunk lease $T_{\text{lease}} =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str`; renewal period $T_{\text{chunk}} =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_chunk_period_str` with a `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_renewal_jitter_str` variation allowance $T_{\text{jitter}}$ (all chosen).

**Math**: The braking term and the ceiling of @eq-nervous-prebrake:
`{python} MachineLeaseBudget.brake_math`
`{python} MachineLeaseBudget.ceiling_math`
Braking, the overheads, and onset travel ($v\,T_{\text{act}} =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.d_onset_str`) already hold `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.prior_total_str` of the clear distance. The lease path, lease plus the tick that notices its expiry plus the bus cycle that delivers the stop, is row 4 of the stopping budget:
`{python} MachineLeaseBudget.row4_math`
`{python} MachineLeaseBudget.total_math`
In time, from the last admission to brake onset, and against the ceiling:
`{python} MachineLeaseBudget.time_math`
Continuous tracking also sets a floor under the lease:
`{python} MachineLeaseBudget.floor_math`

**Systems insight**: A chunk lease is a term in the stopping budget, not a timeout chosen for convenience. Each millisecond added to it costs `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.mm_per_ms_str` of clear distance at the drive limit, distance that the observation age and the stop profile still need, so the lease sits just above its renewal floor rather than anywhere under the ceiling.

:::

The floor is a chosen interval between successful admissions, not a bound that the proposer's $P_{99}$ inference time proves, so it must also cover transport, validation, and mailbox delays, and a missed renewal ends tracking rather than extending it. The `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling_left_str` left under the ceiling is not spare either, because the evidence age through admission and the later terms of the stop profile must still fit inside it.

### Supervisory timers and proposal wire contracts {#sec-nervous-supervisory-timers}

The stalled-proposer timeline starts with the evidence used by the last admitted chunk. That evidence ages through capture, processing, transport, and admission; admission starts the chunk lease but does not reset the evidence timestamp. After a stall, lease expiry is followed by detection on a permission tick, command transport, and physical brake onset. Each elapsed interval enters the stopping budget once. The dispatch-to-admission interval needs its own bound; neither the stored dispatch age nor the newly started lease accounts for it. The evidence-age accounting in @sec-perception must use the same event boundaries, including any processing after a stored dispatch-age value. An earlier evidence deadline or independent hazard check can end authority before lease expiry. The chunk lease bounds continued execution of one admitted motion segment; the goal's validity bounds how long its underlying target remains supported, and neither is the predicted trajectory horizon.

Three independent supervisory timers guard the exchange, and each monitors a distinct failure domain:

1. **The Chunk Lease ($T_{\text{lease}} =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str`):** Bounds how long an admitted proposal may command the actuators. Only a freshly validated, admitted proposal chunk renews the lease. Its duration is derived directly from the physical stopping budget, sitting between the renewal floor and the pre-brake ceiling (\ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}).
2. **The Host Heartbeat ($f_{\text{heartbeat}} =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.f_heartbeat_str`, timeout `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_heartbeat_timeout_str`):** Asserts that the application processor OS kernel and user-space runtime are alive. Expiry of its timeout revokes the active proposal without waiting for the chunk lease. Heartbeat pulses **never renew the chunk lease**, because a live process can easily suffer algorithmic livelock or produce corrupted, out-of-distribution setpoints.
3. **The Microcontroller Self-Watchdog ($T_{\text{self}} =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_self_watchdog_str`):** Monitors whether the permission path completes its required checks within the watchdog interval. The permission loop feeds this hardware watchdog only upon successfully completing all verification checks in a tick; a hung enforcer trips the watchdog even if timer interrupts continue firing (@sec-nervous-fallacies-pitfalls).

A timer feed proves only that the feed path ran. In *Bookout v. Toyota* (2013), a plaintiff expert argued that a timer-tick interrupt kept servicing the watchdog while other tasks could die [@barr2013toyota]; this was an argument made in litigation, not a technical finding, and the NASA and NHTSA investigation identified no electronic cause of large unintended accelerations [@nasa2011toyota].

The payload requirements from @sec-brain describe the candidate motion and the observations supporting it. This chapter adds the transport and authority contract around that payload. The lease is enforced through the **proposal header**\index{Proposal header}, the structured wire contract that allows the permission path to validate candidate trajectories without trusting host software. By contract, the header carries a sequence number, the evidence timestamp of the sensory frame the proposal was computed from (along with clock conversion error bounds), the issue timestamp, the lease expiry, a cryptographic digest of the parent record for lineage tracing, the coordinate frame identifier, the payload type, and a cyclic redundancy check (CRC-32). The payload contains a compact sequence of $H$ waypoints specifying joint positions and velocities. In this selected architecture, the learned policy supplies kinematic intent, the permission path turns the admitted trajectory into position setpoints, and the drives close the velocity and current loops, so this payload carries no raw torque commands. A torque-output policy would require a different payload and corresponding admission checks; its output would still be a proposal. A proposal retains authority only until the earlier of its lease expiry and its evidence deadline, regardless of whether explicit cancellation packets arrive.

Industrial safety communication reached the same header long before learned proposers existed. The functional-safety fieldbus profiles of IEC 61784-3 follow the **black-channel principle**\index{Black-channel principle}: the network, its controllers, and its switches are treated as untrusted, and every safety message carries its own protection, checked only at the two ends [@iec61784-3-2021]. PROFIsafe and Safety over EtherCAT (FSoE) are two such profiles. FSoE guards each safety frame with a CRC against corruption, a sequence number against repetition and loss, a connection identifier against misdelivery, and a watchdog time against delay; a missing or late frame drives the connection to its safe state [@etg2019fsoe]. The proposal header maps onto that list field for field, with the checksum, the sequence number, the payload type and lineage digest, and the lease in the watchdog's place. The board-level link between the application processor and the microcontroller is such a black channel, so the header and its checks travel end to end over it, and nothing about the link itself needs to be trusted. Real-time systems theory supplies the other half of the lineage. Kopetz calls a computer's copy of a changing physical quantity a *real-time image* and calls it *temporally accurate*\index{Temporal accuracy} only for a bounded interval after the observation it was taken from; past that interval the image may no longer describe the world [@kopetz2011real]. The proposal's evidence deadline is that accuracy interval applied to the scene the proposal was computed from, and the lease bounds how long motion derived from it may continue. What this chapter adds to both traditions is where the interval comes from. An industrial safety connection configures its watchdog time, and a real-time image's accuracy interval is set from the dynamics of the quantity it copies, whereas the lease is derived from the plant's stopping budget above and the proposer's renewal floor below (@eq-nervous-prebrake, \ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Byte layout:** The proposal header's and chunk payload's fields, types, and offsets are given in @sec-appendix-systems-wire-header.
:::

Every record that crosses the proposal boundary carries its times on the safety microcontroller's clock. A producer on another clock converts with a versioned mapping and carries that mapping's error bound, which the consumer adds to every age it checks. Calendar time appears only in logs and in a release verdict's expiry, never in an age test.

A record crossing the boundary is protected against three different failures by three different fields. A checksum over header and payload detects accidental corruption; it proves nothing about who wrote the bytes. A digest of the record it was derived from establishes lineage; it is not an authenticator either. A keyed tag appears only where the sender's identity itself confers authority: on operator commands that arrive over a network (@sec-intervention-authenticating-intervention), on the authority log (@sec-intervention-trustworthy-logs), and on offline evidence and release artifacts (@sec-verification-fault-manifest, @sec-release-manifest). Proposals from the learned model carry no keyed tag, because the permission path admits by content, not origin, and a key held by a compromised proposer would authenticate nothing.

The reader's possible failures fall into four classes (@tbl-04-boundary-fallbacks), and none of them lets a failed producer make the permission path wait. The classes keep the exchange from blocking; they do not by themselves contain the plant, because the fallback each one selects still needs bounded timing and a validated stop.

| Failure Class        | Reader Detection Condition                              | Physical Systems Fallback Action                                        | Bounded Response                      |
|:---------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------|
| **Torn / In-Flight** | Odd $c_{\text{start}}$ or changed $c_{\text{end}}$      | Reject current snapshot; use admissible prior chunk or fallback         | One bounded attempt; measure duration |
| **Malformed**        | Checksum or configured command bound fails              | Reject candidate; retain admissible active chunk or use fallback        | Measure check and response            |
| **Stale**            | Past proposal expiry or evidence deadline (local clock) | Reject stale candidate; end active authority if its own deadline passed | Deadline from plant budget            |
| **Missing**          | Sequence gap                                            | Record audit gap; evaluate current record on its own merits             | One tick for flag                     |

: **Boundary contract failure classes and deterministic fallback matrix**: Exchange faults across the proposal boundary by class, with the fallback each selects. Fallback paths are selected without waiting on host recovery. {#tbl-04-boundary-fallbacks tbl-colwidths="[20,30,35,15]"}

### Rate interpolation and boundary fallback execution {#sec-nervous-rate-interpolation}

Rate mismatches between the chunk policy (`{python} MachineTiers.f_chunk_str`) and the `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_tick_str` permission tick introduce three classical systems failure modes: reference lag, aliasing, and buffer starvation. In a discrete-to-continuous conversion, a zero-order hold maintains setpoints constant across the planning period $T_{\text{plan}}$, delivering piecewise-constant position steps rather than a smooth trajectory. Holding each waypoint for a `{python} MachineTiers.t_chunk_period_str` renewal period delays the reference by half that period on average, and each step excites unmodeled mechanical resonances. This delay lies on the reference path, outside the feedback loop: it adds tracking lag, but it does not erode the drive loop's phase margin, which depends only on delays inside the loop (@sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag). Confusing the two leads designers to chase stability problems that are really tracking problems, or the reverse. Across the latched waypoint seam, the real-time enforcer uses a quintic spline bridge that matches position, velocity, and acceleration at both endpoints. Those six boundary conditions provide $C^2$ continuity across chunk transitions, and evaluating the admitted spline at $1\text{ kHz}$ generates smooth velocity setpoints and feedforward acceleration profiles for the joint controllers.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The action chunks this interpolator densifies are generated in @sec-brain-action-chunking.
:::

Aliasing occurs when high-frequency sensor noise folds into low-rate estimators, which the system prevents through analog anti-aliasing filters and digital decimation[^fn-fir-smoothing-delay] within the high-rate microcontroller domain. Sampled-data control designs assume a constant sampling delay; a delay that varies from period to period costs stability margin beyond what its average suggests, so execution jitter must be bounded as well as the mean [@cervin2003control]. They also assume setpoints arrive before the trajectory buffer drains. The permission path enforces these conditions through cycle-deterministic microcontroller interrupts and buffer depth tracking. If the planner stalls and the buffer reaches its final valid waypoint, the permission path rejects stale proposals and requests its validated local deceleration or hold.

[^fn-fir-smoothing-delay]: **Filter Group Delay**: The smoothing that machine learning pipelines apply freely costs delay inside a feedback loop. An $N$-tap moving average, the simplest finite impulse response (FIR) filter, delays its output by $(N-1)/2$ samples, so a `{python} TickDelayBudget.n_fir_str`-tap average on the `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_tick_str` tick lags by `{python} TickDelayBudget.tau_fir_str`. At the `{python} TickDelayBudget.f_c_str` crossover of @sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag that lag spends `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_fir_str`$^\circ$ of phase, `{python} TickDelayBudget.fir_over_mult_str` the whole allowance, which is why decimation filters in a timed path are chosen for delay first and smoothness second. \index{Finite impulse response filter!group delay}

An overrun means something different at each tier of the concurrency hierarchy:

* **Commutation Loop ($20\text{ kHz}$):** Sub-microsecond timing jitter budget. An overrun or overcurrent fault trips inverter gate drives immediately in hardware.
* **Permission Tick ($1\text{ kHz}$):** Update budget of $1000\,\mu\text{s}$. An overrun triggers a deterministic transition to the validated local stopping trajectory.
* **Chunk Policy Stream (`{python} MachineTiers.f_chunk_str`):** Inference latency (`{python} MachineStallTravel.t_chunk_str` P99) is stochastic. Continued execution is limited by the active chunk's remaining lease and evidence validity, not a fresh lease measured from the start of each inference. If authority expires before a replacement is admitted, the enforcer requests the state-matched fallback.
* **Intent Planner (`{python} MachineTiers.f_intent_str`):** Strategic goals expire with their own intent lease, triggering a state-matched station-keeping hold.

Every timed cadence is a deadline, and the lease budget assumes that the tick, the bus cycle, and brake onset meet theirs on every cycle. That assumption needs a worst-case bound on every step between the enforcer's check and the drives, and neither a faster processor nor a longer latency measurement supplies one.

## Real-Time Command Transport and Bus Determinism {#sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses}

The lease budget reserves time for the permission tick and command transport. A measured latency percentile describes how often sampled executions stayed below a threshold; it does not bound an execution that encounters a different combination of competing tasks, memory traffic, or device delays. Even a long run with no deadline miss leaves those cases unresolved.

A response bound instead accounts for the permitted work and waiting along the path under stated operating conditions. This matters twice: delayed feedback consumes the controller's timing margin, and delayed braking consumes clearance before the body can slow. The distinction between event-triggered and scheduled communication [@kopetz2011real] helps identify which waits the analysis must include.

### Response time analysis and execution variance {#sec-nervous-rta-variance}

Response Time Analysis (RTA) bounds a task's response by summing the terms defined in @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning: its own execution, blocking, and interference [@joseph1986finding; @audsley1993applying]. Each term needs an upper bound under the declared operating conditions:
$$R_i = C_i + B_i + I_i \le D_i$$ {#eq-nervous-response-budget}
where $C_i$ is the worst-case execution time (WCET) of task $\tau_i$, $B_i$ is the maximum blocking time spent waiting for lower-priority tasks to leave shared critical sections, $I_i$ is the maximum interference from higher-priority tasks, timer interrupts, and bus transactions that preempt it, and $D_i$ is the relative deadline. Each term has its own kind of evidence. $C_i$ comes either from static analysis of the code on a model of the processor, which is a proven bound, or from the highest execution time measured under stressed conditions, which is only a measured distribution and must be recorded as one. $B_i$ is the longest critical section of any lower-priority task that can hold a resource the task needs. The priority ceiling protocol bounds it. Each lock carries a ceiling, the highest priority of any task that uses it; a task may take a lock only if its priority exceeds the ceilings of all locks other tasks currently hold, and a holder that blocks a higher-priority task inherits that task's priority. Under these rules a task is blocked by at most one lower-priority critical section [@sha1990priority]. A simpler immediate form, which raises a holder to the lock's ceiling as soon as it takes the lock, gives the same bound. $I_i$ is the execution time of every higher-priority task and interrupt that can be released while the task is waiting. Because a longer response admits more higher-priority releases, the exact analysis solves a fixed-point recurrence for $I_i$; @sec-appendix-systems-timers develops it, and @eq-nervous-response-budget is the budget that recurrence fills.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-rta-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RESPONSE-TIME BUDGET FOR THE PERMISSION TICK (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-rta-variance, the RTA example paragraph.
# │ Goal:    Compose R = C + B + I for the tick and compare with its deadline,
# │          then price a missed deadline in base travel.
# │ Show:    250 + 50 + 40 = 340 us <= 400 us deadline, 60 us margin; one
# │          missed period costs 1 ms, or 1.5 mm at the drive limit.
# │ How:     C, D, T from TickVocabulary (AISLE); B and I are scenario bounds.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_display_math, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class TickResponseBudget:
    """R = C + B + I for the permission tick against its deadline."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_wcet = TickVocabulary.t_wcet  # category: chosen (declared WCET)
    t_deadline = TickVocabulary.t_deadline  # category: chosen
    t_period = TickVocabulary.t_period  # category: chosen
    t_block = (
        50 * microsecond
    )  # category: illustrative (longest tick-masking section in lower-priority driver code; the seqlock adds none; scenario bound)
    t_interf = 40 * microsecond  # category: illustrative (timer and bus-interrupt work per response window; scenario bound)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_resp = (t_wcet + t_block + t_interf).to(microsecond)
    t_margin = (t_deadline - t_resp).to(microsecond)
    d_miss = (v * t_period).to(millimeter)  # travel during one extra period of detection delay

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_resp.magnitude - 340.0) < 1e-9, f"Tick response bound drifted: {t_resp}")
    check(abs(t_margin.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Tick response margin drifted: {t_margin}")
    check(t_resp <= t_deadline, "The tick's response bound must meet its deadline")
    check(abs(d_miss.magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Travel per missed period drifted: {d_miss}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_wcet_str = fmt_latency(t_wcet.to(microsecond), unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_block_str = fmt_latency(t_block, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_interf_str = fmt_latency(t_interf, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_resp_str = fmt_latency(t_resp, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_deadline_str = fmt_latency(t_deadline.to(microsecond), unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_miss_str = fmt_length(d_miss, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _us = lambda q: fmt(q, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    resp_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"R = C + B + I = {_us(t_wcet)} + {_us(t_block)} + {_us(t_interf)} = {_us(t_resp)}\ \mu\text{{s}} \le D = {_us(t_deadline)}\ \mu\text{{s}}, \quad D - R = {_us(t_margin)}\ \mu\text{{s}}"
    )
```

Notebook \ref{nbk-nervous-response-margin} applies @eq-nervous-response-budget to the permission tick.

::: {#nbk-nervous-response-margin .callout-notebook title="The response-time margin"}

**Problem**: The permission tick must finish within its deadline after every release. With its declared WCET and illustrative bounds on blocking and interference, does it meet the deadline, and what happens to the margin when one term loses its bound?

**Variables**:

* Declared WCET $C =$ `{python} TickResponseBudget.t_wcet_str` and deadline $D =$ `{python} TickResponseBudget.t_deadline_str` (both chosen).
* Blocking $B =$ `{python} TickResponseBudget.t_block_str`, the longest section in which lower-priority code masks the tick, such as the link driver re-arming its DMA descriptor (illustrative). The mailbox adds nothing to $B$, because the seqlock never makes the tick wait for the receive interrupt.
* Interference $I =$ `{python} TickResponseBudget.t_interf_str`, the timer and bus interrupts that can preempt the tick within one response window (illustrative).

**Math**:
`{python} TickResponseBudget.resp_math`

**Systems insight**: The margin is only as good as the weakest term. Move the mailbox copy into a low-priority task that guards it with a plain mutex, with neither inheritance nor a ceiling, and $B$ has no bound, because medium-priority work can preempt the lock holder indefinitely, the Pathfinder case below; add unscheduled DMA traffic on the tick's memory path and $I$ loses its bound for the same reason. With one unbounded term the tick has no worst-case response time at all, and the stopping budget's $T_{\text{tick}}$ has nothing to stand on.

:::

Neither a small mean latency nor a low processor utilization supplies the missing bound.[^fn-math-liu-layland]

A missed deadline costs the machine differently at each layer. The drives hold the last position setpoint they received for another bus cycle, so their reference lags by a full period, `{python} TickResponseBudget.t_period_str`, not the half period a sample-and-hold contributes; a pattern of misses is jitter, which @cervin2003control analyze as a further loss of margin for any loop closed through the tick. In the safety budget, a delayed tick detects an expired lease or a failed check late, and each `{python} TickResponseBudget.t_period_str` period of that delay costs `{python} TickResponseBudget.d_miss_str` of stopping clearance at the drive limit.

[^fn-math-liu-layland]: **Rate-Monotonic Scheduling**\index{Rate-monotonic scheduling}: @liu1973scheduling established that static-priority rate-monotonic scheduling guarantees periodic task schedulability when total processor utilization satisfies $U \le n(2^{1/n} - 1)$, converging to $\ln(2) \approx 0.693$ for large $n$. The utilization bound is sufficient, not necessary, so a task set that exceeds it may still meet every deadline; with shared-resource blocking and deadlines shorter than periods, only the exact response-time test of @sec-appendix-systems-timers decides.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Deterministic fieldbus jitter bounds provide the execution baseline for heterogeneous placement in @sec-placement-resource-contention.
:::

Bounding these terms requires categorizing every source of execution variance by whether its worst-case bound exists:

1. **Bounded Sources:** Admit analytical upper bounds from hardware specifications. Examples include fixed-pipeline instructions, round-robin bus arbitration, zero-wait-state tightly coupled memory (TCM/SRAM), and vectored interrupt dispatch on a bare-metal microcontroller.
2. **Experimentally Characterized Sources:** Cannot be proven from first principles but can be enveloped under locked hardware configurations. Examples include last-level cache misses under hardware cache line locking, write-buffer drains, periodic DRAM refresh cycles, and thermal throttling under closed-loop active cooling.
3. **Unbounded Sources:** Have no finite mathematical worst-case bound and must be purged from the real-time safety path. Examples include operating system page faults under demand paging, preemptive thread scheduling without priority inheritance (war story \ref{ws-nervous-1997-mars-pathfinder-priority-inversion}), general-purpose heap allocation over fragmented free lists, and unscheduled PCIe DMA crossbar contention.

A timing claim must therefore name the operations permitted inside the critical path. The memory and scheduling controls of @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning remove some sources of delay, and a **zero-allocation static architecture**\index{Zero-allocation static architecture}, which allocates the permission path's buffers and state before operation, removes allocator work from the tick. Neither removes waits on shared hardware, so the response analysis must still account for every remaining wait. The following case shows why a high-priority task alone does not establish a bound.

::: {#ws-nervous-1997-mars-pathfinder-priority-inversion .callout-war-story title="The Mars Pathfinder priority inversion (1997)"}
**Context**: In July 1997, shortly after landing on Mars, the Mars Pathfinder spacecraft's avionics computer ran the VxWorks real-time operating system with preemptive priority-based scheduling across mission tasks [@reeves1997pathfinder].

**Mechanism**: A high-priority thread (`bc_dist`) distributed critical spacecraft bus telemetry, while a low-priority thread (`ASI/MET`) gathered meteorological sensor data through a shared pipe. The mutex that serialized them was not one the application code declared; it was created inside the operating system's `select()` mechanism to protect its list of waiting file descriptors, so the lock was hidden inside a library call [@reeves1997pathfinder]. When `ASI/MET` held the mutex, medium-priority tasks preempted it. Because they outranked the meteorological thread, they kept it from running while `bc_dist` blocked waiting for the mutex it held, an unbounded priority inversion.

**Impact**: The high-priority bus distribution task missed its deadline. When the `bc_sched` task started the next bus cycle and found `bc_dist` unfinished, the flight software reset the computer. Data already collected survived each reset, but the resets recurred until the software was changed.

**Response**: Engineers reproduced the reset on a ground replica of the spacecraft with VxWorks event tracing, then uploaded a patch that enabled priority inheritance [@sha1990priority] on the mutex semaphore.

**Systems lesson**: The medium-priority tasks kept the low-priority mutex holder from running, so the high-priority bus task could not progress. Priority inheritance let the holder finish and release the mutex. In a motor-control path, engineers must bound such blocking time ($B$) or remove the shared lock from the cycle-critical exchange.
:::

### Event-triggered and time-triggered bus architectures {#sec-nervous-fieldbus-architectures}

Command transport contributes to the blocking and interference terms in response-time analysis. Two mechanisms produce different timing obligations. On an event-triggered bus, a node requests transmission when it has data, then competes with other traffic. On a time-triggered bus, a configured schedule reserves access in advance. Neither mechanism supplies a complete response bound without assumptions about payloads, competing traffic, faults, and device processing.

Controller Area Network (CAN) and its Flexible Data-Rate variant (CAN-FD) resolve simultaneous requests by message priority. A higher-priority frame wins arbitration, but it still waits for a frame already in progress to finish. Increasing the data bitrate shortens serialization; it does not remove this non-preemptive blocking. The response budget must include both the bytes sent and the longest permitted wait for access.

EtherCAT instead lets a coordinator send a frame that passes through the drives, whose interface hardware reads commands and inserts feedback as the frame passes. A schedule avoids competition among those drives for transmission, while hardware clock synchronization aligns their local updates. Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) reserves transmission windows on configured Ethernet switches. Its bound depends on the gate schedule, clock error, and traffic admitted to the network. @Sec-appendix-systems-fieldbus supplies the protocol mechanisms and response-time models for evaluating a concrete configuration.

For the mobile manipulator, the design decision is whether the drive commands and feedback fit the allocated bus cycle with enough time left for controller and device response. High-throughput camera links and supervisory middleware need their own budgets, but they must not introduce an unbounded wait into this path. The real-time controller and modular interfaces in @fig-industrial-ethercat-controller illustrate how command coordination can remain local to the drives.

::: {#fig-industrial-ethercat-controller fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Real-time distributed controller with modular I/O**: Dedicated embedded real-time controller and adjacent hardware I/O modules. The unit acts as a deterministic bus coordinator, synchronizing distributed sensor acquisition and motor drive terminals via hardware-scheduled Ethernet telegrams. (Photo: Oleg Yunakov, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Beckhoff_IoT_controller_CX5120.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0)." fig-alt="Photograph of an embedded real-time controller with Ethernet ports and modular I/O terminals."}
![](images/jpg/fig04_real_industrial_ethercat_controller.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

Clock synchronization aligns the instants at which distributed drives sample or update;[^fn-hw-ethercat-dc] it does not measure how long a newly issued command takes to reach them. A tightly aligned set of clocks can still apply an old command if its delivery was delayed. Both command response time and update alignment therefore need explicit bounds.

[^fn-hw-ethercat-dc]: **Distributed Clock**\index{Distributed clock}: EtherCAT Distributed Clocks (DC) synchronize the drive nodes to a reference clock by measuring propagation delays around the ring. Receive-time latches at each node let the coordinator discipline every node's timer, so the hardware `SYNC0` events that start the drives' update cycles occur in close alignment. Clock alignment alone does not bound the complete control cycle, which must also account for controller response time and PWM gate update latency.

### Protocol schedulability comparison between CAN-FD and EtherCAT {#sec-nervous-schedulability-analysis}

On the mobile manipulator the candidate communication links sort strictly by hierarchy:

1. **Board-Level Peripheral Interconnects (SPI, Memory-Mapped I/O):** The serial peripheral interface (SPI), a clocked board-level serial bus, and memory-mapped I/O connect microcontrollers directly to joint encoders, current-shunt ADCs, and gate drivers with sub-microsecond latency ($< 1\,\mu\text{s}$) under a fixed transfer schedule.
2. **Deterministic Drive Command Buses (EtherCAT, TSN Ethernet):** Transports cyclic joint setpoints and sensor feedback across all distributed drive inverters within an allocated $1.0\text{ ms}$ bus cycle ($T_{\text{bus}}$) with sub-microsecond synchronization jitter ($\sigma_{\text{jitter}} < 100\text{ ns}$).
3. **Chassis and Auxiliary Diagnostic Buses (CAN-FD):** Manages lower-rate battery management systems (BMS), environmental sensors, and diagnostic telemetry where priority arbitration is acceptable under verified worst-case bus load.

::: {.column-margin}
<!-- fig-alt below hand-types values because fig-alt cannot hold inline python. Keep them in sync with these cell outputs:
     "nine servo axes"           = FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str
     "1018.8 microseconds"       = FieldbusSchedulability.t_total_one_str (guarded at 1018.8 us)
     "792.4 microseconds"        = FieldbusSchedulability.t_total_arm_str (guarded at 792.4 us)
     "22.0 microseconds"         = FieldbusSchedulability.t_total_ethercat_str (guarded at 22.04 us)

     The SVG is drawn from FieldbusSchedulability by binder/tools/scripts/margin_figures/generate_margin_figures.py;
     its --check fails if this fig-alt loses the 1018.8, 792.4 or 22.0 values (2026-09-29). -->
![](images/svg/margin_fieldbus_cycle_budget_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Scenario bus occupancy for the mobile manipulator's nine servo axes against a dashed red one-millisecond bus cycle: one EtherCAT frame and its forwarding hops take 22.0 microseconds, the arm's CAN FD bus takes 792.4 microseconds, and one CAN FD bus for all axes takes 1018.8 microseconds and crosses the cycle line."}

*One CAN FD bus cannot carry every axis within the cycle; a bus per limb or EtherCAT can.*
:::

None of these bounds belongs to a protocol acronym alone. Each depends on the configured devices, wiring, payload sizes, and schedule. The critical architectural question is whether all servo axes fit within the permission path's bus cycle budget.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-fieldbus-schedulability
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FIELDBUS SERIALIZATION OCCUPANCY: CAN FD VS. ETHERCAT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-nervous-fieldbus-serialization-latency-wcet-schedulability,
# │          @fig-04-fieldbus-evolution, and the margin figure.
# │ Goal:    Quantify bus occupancy for the running machine's servo axes with
# │          command AND feedback frames; full response time needs more terms.
# │ Show:    CAN FD frame (8 B, worst-case stuffing) 56.6 us = 34 bits at
# │          1 Mbps + 113 bits at 5 Mbps; one bus, 18 frames = 1018.8 us > 1 ms;
# │          one bus per limb: arm 14 frames = 792.4 us, base 4 frames =
# │          226.4 us; EtherCAT one frame (16 B/axis) + 9 hops = 22.0 us.
# │ How:     calc_canfd_bus_utilization (ISO 11898-1:2015 frame bits) and
# │          calc_ethercat_cycle_time; axis counts and cycle from RM; PDO
# │          sizes and bit rates are scenario inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_percent, fmt_int, fmt_display_math, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class FieldbusSchedulability:
    """Scenario serialization and forwarding occupancy, not end-to-end schedulability."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    num_axes = RM.servo_axes  # category: chosen (arm joints + drive wheels)
    arm_axes = RM.arm.dofs  # category: datasheet
    cycle_time = RM.fieldbus_cycle  # category: illustrative (EtherCAT cycle, T_bus)

    # Frame parameters below are scenario assumptions (chosen for this comparison)
    pdo_bytes = 8  # category: chosen (position-mode record: 32-bit position + two 16-bit words, each direction)
    frames_per_axis = 2  # category: chosen (one command frame and one feedback frame per axis per cycle)
    canfd_baud_arb = 1.0 * (megabit / second)  # category: chosen (nominal rate)
    canfd_baud_data = 5.0 * (megabit / second)  # category: chosen (data-phase rate)
    ethercat_baud = 100.0 * (megabit / second)  # category: datasheet (100BASE-TX link rate)
    ethercat_header = 64  # category: illustrative
    ethercat_hop = 0.6 * microsecond  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    drive_axes = num_axes - arm_axes
    canfd_kw = dict(
        payload_bytes=pdo_bytes,
        baud_arbitration=canfd_baud_arb,
        baud_data=canfd_baud_data,
        cycle_time=cycle_time,
        frames_per_axis=frames_per_axis,
    )
    one_bus = calc_canfd_bus_utilization(num_axes=num_axes, **canfd_kw)
    arm_bus = calc_canfd_bus_utilization(num_axes=arm_axes, **canfd_kw)
    base_bus = calc_canfd_bus_utilization(num_axes=drive_axes, **canfd_kw)
    ethercat = calc_ethercat_cycle_time(
        num_axes=num_axes,
        bytes_per_axis=frames_per_axis * pdo_bytes,  # command and feedback share one frame
        baud_rate=ethercat_baud,
        header_bytes=ethercat_header,
        hop_delay=ethercat_hop,
        cycle_time=cycle_time,
    )

    t_frame = one_bus["t_tx"]
    t_nom = one_bus["t_nominal"]
    t_dat = one_bus["t_data"]
    bits_nom = one_bus["bits_nominal"]
    bits_dat = one_bus["bits_data"]
    stuff_bits = one_bus["stuff_bits_nominal"] + one_bus["stuff_bits_data"]
    n_frames = one_bus["n_frames"]
    t_total_one = one_bus["t_total_tx"]
    rho_one = one_bus["utilization"]
    n_frames_arm = arm_bus["n_frames"]
    t_total_arm = arm_bus["t_total_tx"]
    rho_arm = arm_bus["utilization"]
    t_left_arm = (cycle_time - t_total_arm).to(microsecond)
    n_frames_base = base_bus["n_frames"]
    t_total_base = base_bus["t_total_tx"]
    rho_base = base_bus["utilization"]

    t_frame_ethercat = ethercat["t_tx"]
    t_hop_ethercat = ethercat["t_forward"]
    t_total_ethercat = ethercat["t_cycle_total"]
    t_margin_ethercat = ethercat["t_margin"]
    rho_ethercat = ethercat["utilization"]

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    # 2026-09-28 (M1): command AND feedback frames, CRC and stuffing in the data
    # phase, 8-byte records; replaces the 9-frame, 64-byte, CRC-at-nominal model.
    check(num_axes == 9 and arm_axes == 7 and drive_axes == 2, f"Axis split drifted: {num_axes} = {arm_axes} + {drive_axes}")
    check(abs(cycle_time.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, f"Bus cycle drifted: {cycle_time}")
    check(bits_nom == 34 and bits_dat == 113, f"CAN FD frame bits drifted: {bits_nom} + {bits_dat}")
    check(abs(t_frame.to(microsecond).magnitude - 56.6) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected CAN FD frame time: {t_frame}")
    check(abs(t_total_one.to(microsecond).magnitude - 1018.8) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected single-bus total: {t_total_one}")
    check(rho_one > 1.0, "One CAN FD bus for nine axes must overrun the 1 ms cycle")
    check(abs(t_total_arm.to(microsecond).magnitude - 792.4) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected arm-bus total: {t_total_arm}")
    check(abs(t_total_base.to(microsecond).magnitude - 226.4) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected base-bus total: {t_total_base}")
    check(rho_arm < 1.0 and rho_base < 1.0, "Per-limb buses must pass the serialization check")
    check(abs(t_total_ethercat.to(microsecond).magnitude - 22.04) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected EtherCAT total: {t_total_ethercat}")
    check(abs(t_margin_ethercat.to(microsecond).magnitude - 977.96) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected unallocated bus time: {t_margin_ethercat}")
    check(rho_ethercat < 0.05, "EtherCAT utilization must be under 5%")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    num_axes_str = fmt_int(num_axes)
    arm_axes_str = fmt_int(arm_axes)
    drive_axes_str = fmt_int(drive_axes)
    cycle_time_str = fmt_latency(cycle_time, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    pdo_bytes_str = fmt_int(pdo_bytes)

    bits_nom_str = fmt_int(bits_nom)
    bits_dat_str = fmt_int(bits_dat)
    stuff_bits_str = fmt_int(stuff_bits)
    t_frame_str = fmt_latency(t_frame, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    n_frames_str = fmt_int(n_frames)
    t_total_one_str = fmt_latency(t_total_one, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    rho_one_pct_str = fmt_percent(rho_one, precision=1, style="prose")
    n_frames_arm_str = fmt_int(n_frames_arm)
    t_total_arm_str = fmt_latency(t_total_arm, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    rho_arm_pct_str = fmt_percent(rho_arm, precision=1, style="prose")
    t_left_arm_str = fmt_latency(t_left_arm, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    n_frames_base_str = fmt_int(n_frames_base)
    t_total_base_str = fmt_latency(t_total_base, unit=microsecond, precision=1)

    t_total_ethercat_str = fmt_latency(t_total_ethercat, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_margin_ethercat_str = fmt_latency(t_margin_ethercat, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    rho_ethercat_pct_str = fmt_percent(rho_ethercat, precision=1, style="prose")
    ethercat_hop_str = fmt_latency(ethercat_hop, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    ethercat_header_str = fmt_int(ethercat_header)

    _us1 = lambda q: fmt(q, unit=microsecond, precision=1, commas=False)
    canfd_frame_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{frame}}}} = \frac{{{bits_nom}\ \text{{bits}}}}{{{fmt(canfd_baud_arb, unit=megabit / second, precision=0)}\ \text{{Mbps}}}} + \frac{{{bits_dat}\ \text{{bits}}}}{{{fmt(canfd_baud_data, unit=megabit / second, precision=0)}\ \text{{Mbps}}}} = {fmt(t_nom, unit=microsecond, precision=0)} + {_us1(t_dat)} = {_us1(t_frame)}\ \mu\text{{s}}"
    )
    canfd_bus_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"{n_frames} \times {_us1(t_frame)} = {_us1(t_total_one)}\ \mu\text{{s}} > {fmt(cycle_time, unit=microsecond, precision=0, commas=False)}\ \mu\text{{s}}, \qquad {n_frames_arm} \times {_us1(t_frame)} = {_us1(t_total_arm)}\ \mu\text{{s}}"
    )
    ethercat_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\frac{{({ethercat_header} + {num_axes} \times {frames_per_axis * pdo_bytes})\ \text{{B}} \times 8}}{{{fmt(ethercat_baud, unit=megabit / second, precision=0)}\ \text{{Mbps}}}} + {num_axes} \times {_us1(ethercat_hop)}\ \mu\text{{s}} = {fmt(t_frame_ethercat, unit=microsecond, precision=2)} + {_us1(t_hop_ethercat)} = {fmt(t_total_ethercat, unit=microsecond, precision=2)}\ \mu\text{{s}}"
    )
```

::: {#nbk-nervous-fieldbus-serialization-latency-wcet-schedulability .callout-notebook title="Fieldbus serialization before schedulability"}

**Problem**: The mobile manipulator's permission path exchanges position setpoints and feedback with its servo axes once per bus cycle. How much of that cycle do CAN FD frames, or one EtherCAT frame, occupy before controller and device delays are counted, and which buses pass this necessary check?

**Variables**:

* `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` servo axes, `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.arm_axes_str` arm joints and `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.drive_axes_str` drive wheels (datasheet), exchanged every `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.cycle_time_str` bus cycle (illustrative).
* An `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.pdo_bytes_str`-byte record per axis in each direction, a 32-bit position and two 16-bit words (chosen).
* CAN FD at $1\text{ Mbps}$ nominal and $5\text{ Mbps}$ in the data phase (chosen). A CAN frame carries one message, so each axis needs a command frame and a feedback frame. The arbitration field and the trailer run at the nominal rate, `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.bits_nom_str` bits; the data-length code, payload, stuff count, and 17-bit CRC run at the data rate, `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.bits_dat_str` bits [@iso11898-1-2015; @bosch2012canfd]. Both counts include the worst-case `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.stuff_bits_str` dynamic stuff bits, because a bound must assume the bit pattern that lengthens the frame most.
* EtherCAT at $100\text{ Mbps}$ (datasheet), one frame carrying every axis's command and feedback with a `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.ethercat_header_str`-byte header, and a forwarding delay of `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.ethercat_hop_str` per node, the shift-register pass-through of a slave controller that never buffers the frame (both illustrative).

**Math**: One CAN FD frame, then all frames on one bus and on an arm bus:
`{python} FieldbusSchedulability.canfd_frame_math`
`{python} FieldbusSchedulability.canfd_bus_math`
The base's `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.n_frames_base_str` frames take `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_total_base_str`. For EtherCAT, serialization plus forwarding:
`{python} FieldbusSchedulability.ethercat_math`

**Result**: One CAN FD bus fills `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.rho_one_pct_str` of the cycle on serialization alone. A bus per limb passes, the arm bus at `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.rho_arm_pct_str` with `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_left_arm_str` left for blocking, competing frames, and retransmissions. EtherCAT occupies `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.rho_ethercat_pct_str` and leaves `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_margin_ethercat_str` unallocated by this calculation.

**Systems insight**: CAN FD's fast data phase does not rescue a single bus, because every frame still pays its arbitration and trailer bits at the nominal rate and CAN needs two frames per axis where EtherCAT needs one frame for all of them. Neither calculation is a response bound: arbitration, non-preemptive blocking, and retransmission belong in the CAN FD analysis, and coordinator, device, and fault-response delays in the EtherCAT analysis. Each delay that survives into the command path costs stopping clearance as $v\,\Delta t_{\text{bus}}$.

:::

### Bandwidth and jitter trade-offs on the synchronization frontier {#sec-nervous-synchronization-frontier}

The serialization example separates three quantities that a bus specification can otherwise blur. Bandwidth bounds how many bytes fit in an interval. Command response time includes waiting, transmission, and processing before a drive can act. Synchronization jitter bounds variation in the relative timing of distributed updates. A design can improve one while leaving another unchanged.

The configured scenario in @fig-04-fieldbus-evolution compares only serialization and forwarding occupancy against the allocated bus cycle. It rejects a single CAN FD bus for all nine axes before a full response analysis and leaves the per-limb buses and EtherCAT to be evaluated. It supplies neither a synchronization-jitter bound nor a complete response bound. A CAN-FD schedule needs a bound on competing frames and non-preemptive blocking; an EtherCAT path needs frame, forwarding, and device delays; a TSN schedule needs reserved windows and clock-error allowances.[^fn-net-tsn-fieldbus] These are inputs to the response calculation, not guarantees obtained by selecting a protocol name.

Freshness adds a further requirement. Even a command delivered within its transport bound may have been computed from old evidence. The proposal header's evidence timestamp and expiry therefore remain necessary on a synchronized network. The transport budget must leave room for the command's physical response, and the permission path must refuse a command whose authority has ended.

[^fn-net-tsn-fieldbus]: **Time-Sensitive Networking**\index{Time-sensitive networking}: IEEE 802.1Qbv Time-Sensitive Networking establishes deterministic Ethernet communication by configuring time-aware traffic shapers across network switches. High-priority control frames execute within dedicated, pre-scheduled transmission windows, while asynchronous high-bandwidth payloads (such as uncompressed camera streams) are temporarily gated. This scheduled time-division multiplexing allows vision telemetry and microsecond servo commands to coexist over a unified physical link without packet collision or buffer bloat.

::: {#fig-04-fieldbus-evolution fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Scenario bus occupancy before response qualification**: Modeled serialization and forwarding terms for the configured servo-axis example, command and feedback included, compared with the allocated bus cycle. One CAN FD bus for all axes exceeds the allocation before other delays are counted. A CAN FD bus per limb and EtherCAT leave unallocated time, but controller response, competing traffic, device delays, and fault allowances still need qualification. These calculated values are not measured end-to-end response or synchronization bounds." fig-alt="Horizontal bars compare modeled occupancy for one CAN FD bus carrying all axes, a CAN FD bus for the arm, a CAN FD bus for the base, and EtherCAT. The single CAN FD bus exceeds the vertical line marking the allocated bus cycle; the other bars remain below it."}

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-checkpoint-estimates
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHECKPOINT ESTIMATE GIVENS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @chk-nervous-response-bounds and @chk-nervous-hardware-invariants.
# │ Goal:    Print the givens of the checkpoints' estimate items and guard the
# │          verdict each item expects, without printing the answer.
# │ Show:    blocking 50 -> 120 us (tick misses 400 us by 10 us); 56.6 us
# │          frames, two per axis (8 axes per 1 ms bus); lease 60 -> 100 ms
# │          (60 mm at 1.5 m/s).
# │ How:     Reuses TickResponseBudget, FieldbusSchedulability, and
# │          MachineLeaseBudget; the two changed values are checkpoint givens.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, check

class CheckpointEstimates:
    """Givens for the checkpoint estimate items, with guards on their verdicts."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_block_new = 120 * microsecond  # category: illustrative (checkpoint given: a longer tick-masking section)
    t_lease_new = 100 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (checkpoint given: a lengthened lease)
    t_block = TickResponseBudget.t_block  # category: illustrative
    t_wcet = TickResponseBudget.t_wcet  # category: chosen
    t_interf = TickResponseBudget.t_interf  # category: illustrative
    t_deadline = TickResponseBudget.t_deadline  # category: chosen
    t_frame = FieldbusSchedulability.t_frame  # category: derived
    cycle = FieldbusSchedulability.cycle_time  # category: illustrative
    t_lease = MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease  # category: chosen
    v = MachineLeaseBudget.v  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_resp_new = (t_wcet + t_block_new + t_interf).to(microsecond)
    axes_per_bus = int((cycle / (2 * t_frame)).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    d_extra = (v * (t_lease_new - t_lease)).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(t_resp_new > t_deadline, "Checkpoint: the longer blocking section must break the deadline.")
    check(abs((t_resp_new - t_deadline).to(microsecond).magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9, f"Checkpoint deadline miss drifted: {t_resp_new}")
    check(axes_per_bus == 8, f"Checkpoint: axes per CAN FD bus drifted: {axes_per_bus}")
    check(abs(d_extra.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Checkpoint lease cost drifted: {d_extra}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_block_str = fmt_latency(t_block, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_block_new_str = fmt_latency(t_block_new, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_deadline_str = fmt_latency(t_deadline.to(microsecond), unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_frame_str = fmt_latency(t_frame, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    cycle_str = fmt_latency(cycle, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_new_str = fmt_latency(t_lease_new, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
```

The lease budget counts the permission tick and the bus cycle as bounded terms. These items test whether you can supply the bounds it assumes.

- [ ] **Percentile vs. bound**: Can you explain why a measured $P_{99}$ response time, however long the test that produced it, may enter the handoff record only as a measured distribution and never as a proven bound?
- [ ] **Response-time estimate**: If the longest tick-masking section in the link driver grew from `{python} CheckpointEstimates.t_block_str` to `{python} CheckpointEstimates.t_block_new_str`, with the tick's WCET and interference unchanged, would the tick still meet its `{python} CheckpointEstimates.t_deadline_str` deadline, and by how much would it pass or miss?
- [ ] **Bus occupancy estimate**: With one command frame and one feedback frame per axis at `{python} CheckpointEstimates.t_frame_str` each, how many axes can one CAN FD bus serve within a `{python} CheckpointEstimates.cycle_str` cycle before any blocking is counted?
- [ ] **Synchronization vs. latency**: Can you explain why tightly synchronized drive clocks do not bound how long a newly issued command takes to reach the drives?
