A bounded path delivers each command to the drives within its cycle, but it is indifferent to which commands it carries. Which processor may place a command on that path, and what that processor must check first, is a question of authority rather than timing.

## Actuation Authority {#sec-nervous-actuation-authority}

A mailbox cannot protect the mobile manipulator if the host also has a diagnostic route that writes directly to a drive. The partition established in @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning therefore needs exclusive control over every path that can energize the windings. Actuation authority is this physical ability to change drive commands, including PWM registers, current references, and bridge-enable signals. The host publishes proposals; the permission path alone admits commands to those interfaces (@fig-04-privilege-enforcer-registers).

::: {#fig-04-privilege-enforcer-registers fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Hardware proposal boundary**: (a) The application processor proposes across a black-channel board link into the safety microcontroller's own double buffer; the permission path on that microcontroller is the sole writer of the drive registers and can trip a drive inhibit. (b) When the application processor can write the drive registers directly, an unchecked write reaches the motors, and proposer and drives share a single failure domain." fig-alt="Two panels. (a) Separate permission path: a dashed bronze application processor box, learned proposers with no drive access, sends proposal p t through a dashed black-channel board link with CRC and sequence into a safety MCU container, which has its own memory and is the sole writer of drive registers. Inside it, an MCU-local double buffer feeds the permission path at a 1 kHz tick, which checks state, freshness, and lease. The permission path sends admitted command u t to drive registers and then drives and motors; a red trip line from the permission path sends drive inhibit to the drives and motors. (b) Collapsed, host writes drives: inside a red dashed box labeled one failure domain, the application processor sends an unchecked register write straight to the drive registers, which feed the drives and motors."}
![](images/svg/fig04_privilege_enforcer_registers.svg){width="90%"}
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Actuator override masking registers implement the hardware preemption tiers formulated in @sec-intervention-authority-log.
:::

The microcontroller continuously evaluates physical safety invariants: verifying that commanded joint positions lie within physical reach envelopes, that joint velocities do not exceed certified limits, and that projected decelerations remain safely within dynamic stopping clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$). If a proposal satisfies all invariants, the microcontroller grants execution permission and interpolates waypoints into position setpoints for each bus cycle, which the drives execute through their own velocity and current loops. An invalid or expired candidate is refused ($\bot$); it does not automatically revoke a different active chunk. The active chunk continues only while its own state, evidence, and lease remain valid. When those checks fail, the enforcer ends its authority and requests a controlled deceleration or hold. A separate hardware trip zone can remove drive torque on a fault; opening switches does not itself brake moving mass.[^fn-hw-tripzone-break]

[^fn-hw-tripzone-break]: **Hardware Trip Zone**\index{Hardware trip zone}: Microcontroller hardware trip zones couple analog overcurrent and overvoltage comparators directly to timer output logic. Upon fault detection, configured trip logic may force gate signals high-impedance or activate a validated braking mode. These have different mechanical consequences: torque removal can leave the plant coasting, while dynamic braking requires a rated energy path.

By virtue of the causal boundary established in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary, the enforcer treats the origin of an aberrant proposal as irrelevant. A remote memory exploit in an operating system daemon, an adversarial camera perturbation inducing model hallucination, and an arithmetic overflow in a neural matrix multiplier all produce the same boundary event, an invalid proposal packet. Because the enforcer evaluates invariant bounds against physical sensor feedback from optical encoders and current shunts rather than inspecting neural network weights, it needs no model of why a proposal went wrong, and the host, which cannot write actuator registers directly, has no path around it. Protection against a compromised host still depends on independent sensing, a correct limit model, actuator capability, and a feasible fallback.

Controlled stopping and torque removal impose different obligations. Powered braking uses the drives to remove motion before torque is disabled; immediate torque removal can leave a base coasting or a loaded arm falling. Holding position requires continued torque or a separately rated restraint. The stop-category comparison in @sec-enforcement-stop-categories develops these alternatives. At this interface, the requirement is to specify the physical response and reserve the time and energy it needs.

The refusal carries its own physical cost. If the enforcer rejects an invalid proposal and commands dynamic braking on a fast-moving joint, the braking path must have enough torque, clearance, and thermal capacity to arrest the mass. Over a braking interval of hundreds of milliseconds, the winding resistance, brake resistor, or friction that forms that path must absorb the joint's kinetic energy within the thermal limits of @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles, without damaging the winding insulation or letting the mass coast past its clearance. @Sec-appendix-systems-stopping derives the stopping distance, and @sec-appendix-systems-actuators develops the winding-heating and thermal-limit models.

If the enforcer itself hangs, it may be unable to request that controlled response. An out-of-band interlock must then trigger the separately qualified fault response. Safe Torque Off (STO) prevents torque-producing drive signals; it does not isolate the main supply or guarantee that a moving load stops within the normal powered-braking budget.[^fn-std-iec61800-sto] A separate contactor can provide supply isolation, and a rated brake or other restraint may be needed to contain the resulting motion. The illustrated interlock (@fig-real-estop) makes the torque-inhibit path independent of the proposal software; qualification must still establish its behavior under shared power, clock, and wiring faults.

[^fn-std-iec61800-sto]: **Safe Torque Off (STO)**\index{Safe torque off}: An STO implementation removes torque-producing drive signals through a hardware interlock. An IEC 61800-5-2 integrity rating depends on the actual devices, diagnostic coverage, wiring, and validation, not on the circuit pattern alone [@iec61800part52].

::: {#fig-real-estop fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative out-of-band interlock and STO path**: Each emergency-stop contact holds its own force-guided relay, and each relay's enable contact holds one of the drive's two STO inputs, so a single welded contact or shorted wire leaves the other channel able to remove torque. The EDM contacts report a relay that failed to release before restart. Removing torque leaves the motor free to coast; the spring-applied brake is a separate circuit that clamps when its supply is removed. The diagram shows a hardware response path, not a certified integrity level or a stopping distance (synthesized from ISO 13849-1 and IEC 61800-5-2)." fig-alt="Two-channel schematic. A red positive-break E-stop is mechanically linked to two normally closed contacts, S1 and S2, each fed from 24 volts. S1 feeds the coil of force-guided relay K1 and S2 the coil of relay K2; each relay has a normally open enable contact and a normally closed EDM contact. K1 sends STO1 enable and K2 sends STO2 enable to two STO terminals on the drive, which feed the gate-drive supply and then the inverter bridge driving motor M. A red tag above the motor reads tau equals 0, and a note below reads may coast. The two EDM contacts are wired in series with a dashed teal line to a reset monitor, restart only if K1 and K2 released. At the bottom, a brake supply on its own circuit, via K1 and K2, feeds a spring brake that clamps on power loss and acts on the motor shaft. A note reads hardware only, no processor in this path."}
![](images/svg/fig04_sto_safety_circuit.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The switch and monitored relay channels detect an emergency input or channel disagreement and inhibit drive torque. The spring-applied holding brake provides a separate restraint. Its name does not establish a dynamic stopping capability: normal powered deceleration applies it after rest, while emergency application during motion needs its own energy and stopping-distance qualification. The response selection and sequencing in @sec-enforcement-stop-categories depend on those physical capabilities.

::: {#psp-nervous-hardware-authority .callout-perspective title="Hardware authority invariant"}
If an unverified learned policy has direct memory-mapped write access to actuator gate-driver registers, the machine has no safety layer, and its next out-of-distribution input reaches the motors unchecked.
:::

Write privilege is therefore a physical fact about wires and registers, not a software permission, and the Brain holds none of it. The privilege settles who may change a drive command; it leaves open what a proposal may ask the drive to do.

### What a proposal may command {#sec-nervous-command-interface}

A drive accepts a setpoint at one of several levels of its own control cascade: position, velocity, or current, with the current loop innermost. The level at which a proposal enters decides which physical quantities the drive regulates by itself and which the permission path must check before it admits the command. The choice is therefore part of the proposal boundary, not a detail of the drive configuration. Four command interfaces cover current practice, and each leaves a different residue to the permission path.

A *position target* $q_{\text{des}}$ hands the drive's position, velocity, and current loops the whole task of tracking. The drive enforces its configured speed and current limits, so the permission path checks the target against the reach envelope, the step between successive targets (which the loop gains turn into velocity and torque), and the stopping clearance. What a position target cannot express is how hard to push. Against a rigid obstacle, a stiff position loop treats the contact as an error to be removed and raises current until the drive saturates; perspective \ref{psp-body-impedance-control} priced that rise on the machine's cage-door latch.

A *velocity target* $\dot{q}_{\text{des}}$ leaves position to the proposer. The permission path can no longer check a stated endpoint. It must integrate the commanded velocity over the active lease to predict where the joint will be when authority expires, and check the reach envelope and the stopping distance against that prediction. Contact force is again unregulated.

A *torque target* $\tau_{\text{des}}$, delivered as a current reference, bypasses both outer loops. The drive regulates only winding current, so every kinematic quantity, including the stopping distance itself, becomes a consequence of the plant's dynamics rather than of a setpoint. The permission path must predict motion from a model of the plant, bound the torque slew, and bound the energy the command can inject. This interface leaves the permission path the most to check and the least stated intent to check it against; what can still be guaranteed when a learned policy commands torque at control rate is the subject of @sec-enforcement-thesis-bends.

An *impedance target* specifies an equilibrium together with a stiffness $K_p$ and a damping $K_d$, so that the drive behaves as a virtual spring-damper, $F = K_p (x_{\text{des}} - x) + K_d (\dot{x}_{\text{des}} - \dot{x})$ [@hogan1985impedance]. Its dual, an *admittance target*, measures the contact force and moves in response to it. Either interface regulates the relation between motion and force that the other three leave to chance, which is why contact tasks use it. The permission path must then check the gains as well as the equilibrium. Under quasi-static contact, the stiffness times the largest displacement the environment can impose bounds the steady force, so a stiffness raised past what the contact tolerates is as inadmissible as a target outside the reach envelope. The gains do not bound the first impact, which also depends on approach speed, passive compliance, and actuator bandwidth; the energy and force barriers of @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact cover what the gains leave open.

On the mobile manipulator the permission path admits position setpoints, interpolated from admitted waypoints at each bus cycle, and the drives close their velocity and current loops beneath them. When the arm must push against the latch spring of the cage door, the command gains a stiffness and damping, and the admitted gains become part of what the tick checks. No interface narrows the permission path's duty to zero. Moving the command inward, from position toward torque, removes stated intent that the path could check and adds dynamics that it must predict.

Write privilege and a narrow command interface protect the plant only while the enforcer stays independent of the processor whose proposals it refuses. If the two share a clock, a rail, or a memory bus, a fault in the proposer can silence the enforcer without ever writing to a drive.

## Hardware Isolation and Fault Containment {#sec-nervous-hardware-isolation}

A separate permission processor can still reset when an accelerator burst pulls down a supply it shares with the proposer. It can also miss a tick while waiting for a memory bus it shares. The partition therefore needs evidence about common resources, not another software boundary. Execution, timing, power, and memory define the fault paths that must be examined.

Private execution resources, independent timing references, isolated power rails, and bounded memory access can contain these paths.[^fn-std-iso26262-ffi] Where resources remain shared, the design must show that interference and the declared common-cause faults cannot defeat the permission deadline or its qualified fallback.

[^fn-std-iso26262-ffi]: **Freedom from Interference (FFI)**\index{Freedom from interference}: ISO 26262 defines FFI in its vocabulary, Part 1, as the absence of cascading failures between two or more elements that could lead to the violation of a safety requirement [@iso26262]. Part 6 lists the software interference it covers (timing and execution, memory, and exchange of information), whereas shared power, clocks, and heat are common-cause and cascading faults that Part 9 treats in its dependent-failure analysis and that IEC 61508 addresses as independence between elements [@iec61508-2-2010]. A neural policy sharing silicon with the permission path therefore needs both arguments, FFI for its software and a dependent-failure analysis for the resources underneath.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-permission-rail
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SHARED DRIVE BUS VS. THE HELD-UP PERMISSION RAIL (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-hardware-isolation, the design-choice paragraph
# │          (the full four-coupling inventory lives in @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die).
# │ Goal:    Name the bus the application processor shares with the drives and
# │          the isolated, held-up rail the permission path runs on instead.
# │ Show:    47.7 V nominal drive bus, 42 V depleted, the application
# │          processor's converter locking out at 33 V, 2 s hold-up.
# │ How:     Registry fields on RM (M6: 48 V drive bus, MiR250-class pack,
# │          MEAN WELL DDR-240C-24 converter). The sustained sag screen is
# │          derived in @sec-body-power-integrity, and the hold-up is sized in
# │          @sec-body-permission-rail-isolation.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_voltage, fmt_latency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PermissionRail:
    """The permission path's isolated, held-up rail beside the shared drive bus."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_bus_nom = RM.drive_bus_nominal  # category: datasheet (48 V-class pack, nominal)
    v_bus_low = RM.drive_bus_battery_low  # category: datasheet (pack minimum)
    v_uvlo = RM.drive_bus_uvlo  # category: datasheet (converter input lockout)
    t_holdup = RM.permission_rail_holdup  # category: chosen (permission-rail hold-up)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_headroom_low = (v_bus_low - v_uvlo).to(volt)  # headroom a depleted pack starts with

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_bus_nom.to(volt).magnitude - 47.7) < 1e-9, f"Drive bus nominal drifted: {v_bus_nom}")
    check(abs(v_uvlo.to(volt).magnitude - 33.0) < 1e-9, f"Converter lockout drifted: {v_uvlo}")
    check(abs(t_holdup.to(second).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Permission-rail hold-up drifted: {t_holdup}")
    check(abs(v_headroom_low.magnitude - 9.0) < 1e-9, "Even a depleted pack starts 9 V above the converter lockout")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_bus_nom_str = fmt_voltage(v_bus_nom, unit=volt, precision=1)
    v_uvlo_str = fmt_voltage(v_uvlo, unit=volt, precision=0)
    t_holdup_str = fmt_latency(t_holdup, unit=second, precision=0)
```

The machine's two-processor hypothesis answers each path with a design choice. The permission path runs from its own memory behind a board link and on its own oscillator, and it draws from the isolated rail of @sec-body-archetype-matrix rather than from the `{python} PermissionRail.v_bus_nom_str` drive bus that feeds the application processor. That rail is held up with diode-isolated storage capacitors for `{python} PermissionRail.t_holdup_str`, so a supply fault that locks out the host's converter at `{python} PermissionRail.v_uvlo_str` leaves the safety microcontroller powered long enough to receive the undervoltage flag and request a fallback while the host reboots. Continued logic power does not guarantee braking power or torque. A controlled stop still requires sufficient drive power, braking capability, and clearance; if those are unavailable, the design needs a qualified unpowered response whose brake engagement and resulting motion fit the physical budget. Each of these choices is a claim rather than a finding. @Sec-placement-two-paths-one-die inventories the four couplings (memory, power, heat, and clock) that the board must cut, shows how each moves inside one package on a shared die, and names the fault injections that would refute the separation. The obligation here is to carry each dependency into the handoff record.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_substrate_blast_radius.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Blast-radius sketch: a red square labeled 48 V bus transient sends arrows to four red dots labeled host lockout 33 V, thermal coupling, DMA starvation, and clock jitter. A dashed branch toward a green dot labeled permission rail ends at a green bar before reaching it."}

*A transient on the shared rail reaches every load that draws from it; the permission path rides through on its own isolated, held-up rail.*
:::

Isolation keeps the permission path running when the proposer fails; what the path must then do depends on how the proposer failed. It distinguishes two failure modes, unresponsiveness and corruption. Unresponsiveness occurs when an inference pipeline hangs, a scheduling deadline is missed, or operating system memory fragmentation blocks execution, producing no output. A host failure can trip the heartbeat timer; a live host that stops publishing admissible chunks instead reaches the active chunk's lease or evidence deadline. These are the distinct timer obligations established in @sec-nervous-supervisory-timers.

Corruption occurs when the proposer remains fully active and passes its heartbeat deadline, but generates kinematically impossible setpoints, discontinuous velocity requests, or numerical infinities resulting from out-of-distribution visual inputs or matrix overflow. The enforcer answers the two failures through separate mechanisms. A missing fresh chunk or a missed heartbeat revokes the proposal when its timer expires, whereas corruption triggers an immediate invariant rejection on the arrival of the malformed proposal packet.

The timer distinction now has a physical consequence. A live heartbeat cannot justify continued tracking after the active chunk expires; the stopping-budget lease ends that authority independently. The coupled budget in @sec-nervous-coupled-budget checks whether the chunk policy can supply renewals often enough. It also shows why the slower intent model must supply goals rather than hold the motion lease itself.

When active authority ends and no admissible continuation remains, the permission path executes an explicit degradation strategy rather than an unconditioned power cut, because cutting power hands a moving actuator to whichever unpowered state its drive falls into (@sec-body-power-integrity), and none of those states is a controlled stop. The permission path selects degradation from the current physical state and the responses still feasible there. An optional short continuation of the last validated trajectory is permissible only while its state, evidence, chunk lease, and stopping margin remain valid. After expiry, any separately authorized fallback delay $T_{\text{hold}}$ enters $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ and must fit in the `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling_left_str` of pre-brake ceiling that the lease path and brake onset leave at the drive limit (\ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}); the enforcer must begin braking sooner if the measured bounds of the remaining terms do not fit. The permission path requests controlled deceleration before that budget is exhausted using the available torque and thermal budget established in @sec-body-actuator-limits. It reaches rest only if clearance and braking capability remain sufficient. A gravity-loaded arm may require a rated mechanical holding brake after motion has been arrested.

Once the physical plant is brought to a complete, stationary halt, the architecture executes a **recovery handshake**\index{Recovery handshake} before restoring autonomous proposal authority. The safety microcontroller asserts a persistent `FAULT_HELD` latch in a status word it owns and reports the exact physical rest pose $(\mathbf{q}_{\text{rest}}, \dot{\mathbf{q}} = \mathbf{0})$. The application processor must discard stale action chunks, invalidate state tied to the interrupted motion, ingest fresh observations tagged with new hardware timestamps, and publish a re-synchronized chunk proposal.

Recovery must also invalidate proposal-side state that assumes the pre-fault motion continued. For an autoregressive policy, this can include cached tokens or a key-value (KV) attention cache; the required reset depends on what the model stores and how it incorporates fresh observations. A cache flush alone does not establish physical continuity. The microcontroller verifies that the initial waypoint of the new proposal matches the physical rest state within a strict spatial epsilon ($||\mathbf{a}_0 - \mathbf{q}_{\text{rest}}|| \le \epsilon_{\text{sync}}$) before releasing the fault latch and restoring proposal authority.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Real-time bus fault-recovery state machines are verified via hardware fault-injection in @sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection.
:::

Independence is validated against identified common-cause faults rather than read off a block diagram, and the lease that bounds a stopped proposer comes from the stopping margin that remains after detection and actuation delays. Both defenses bound a proposer that stops or fails, which leaves open whether a proposer running at the enforcer's own rate still needs a separate check.

## Invariant Checking {#sec-nervous-invariant-checking}

A proposer fast enough to keep pace with the permission tick invites a shortcut. Learned locomotion controllers already emit joint targets within an order of magnitude of a millisecond, and a designer may be tempted to let such a policy write the motor registers directly. Rate does not confer authority. A fast network emitting joint targets or torques carries the same statistical uncertainty as a large model generating waypoints a few times a second, and even when policy and enforcer share one period, the network's output remains a proposal that must pass the proposal boundary of @sec-boundary-machine-model before it changes current in a winding. What the permission path can still guarantee when a learned policy commands at control rate, and what it gives up, is examined in @sec-enforcement-thesis-bends.

The interface must reject an inadmissible candidate without waiting for the producer, and recheck the active command against current physical state. Position and velocity limits ($\mathbf{q} \in [\mathbf{q}_{\min}, \mathbf{q}_{\max}]$ and $|\dot{\mathbf{q}}| \le \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\max}$) are necessary but do not by themselves establish a feasible stop. A torque-slew constraint, $|\dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}}| = |(\boldsymbol{\tau}_k - \boldsymbol{\tau}_{k-1})/\Delta t| \le \dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{\max}$, can limit command changes, but a corrected command must still satisfy the other physical limits. Contact may additionally require accounting for exchanged energy, $\int \boldsymbol{\tau}^T \dot{\mathbf{q}}\,dt$; @sec-appendix-control-passivity develops that background.

Choosing and composing those filters requires the state and motion models developed later in the volume. @Sec-enforcement constructs the admissibility calculation and selects a feasible continuation, hold, or stop. The architectural result here is its execution contract: checks must finish within their allocated response time, use qualified physical evidence, and retain sole actuator authority. Neither fast inference nor a fast rejection routine establishes that contract on its own.

The same reasoning covers the one proposer that is not learned. A remote operator is a third proposer. Its commands pass the same permission path, and network delay spends the same pre-brake budget (@sec-intervention-human-authority). Neither speed nor a human origin gives a proposal authority; only passing the permission path's checks does, and each check spends part of a budget that the next section lays out handoff by handoff.

::: {#chk-nervous-hardware-invariants .callout-checkpoint title="Hardware isolation and invariant checking"}

Before turning to the handoffs between proposer and actuator, verify your understanding of the exchange, hardware isolation, and pre-actuation invariant defenses:

- [ ] **Nonblocking exchange**: Can you explain how the seqlock reader detects a torn read in one bounded attempt, and why a writer stopped mid-write cannot extend the active spline's state, evidence, or lease validity?
- [ ] **Independence as a hypothesis**: Can you state the independence requirement the permission path must meet, and explain why the two-processor split satisfies it only once loaded tests on the machine's silicon support the claim?
- [ ] **Chunk lease cost**: Can you explain why the chunk lease must be sized from stopping distance and clearance rather than chosen as a software timeout, why a heartbeat never renews it, and how much clear distance lengthening it from `{python} CheckpointEstimates.t_lease_str` to `{python} CheckpointEstimates.t_lease_new_str` would spend at the `{python} CheckpointEstimates.v_str` drive limit?
- [ ] **Command interface**: Can you state what the permission path must check or predict for a position, a velocity, a torque, and an impedance target, and why a velocity target leaves it to predict motion over the whole lease?
- [ ] **Rate matching and authority**: Can you explain why a policy that runs at the plant's own rate still produces only proposals, and what timing, state, and fallback obligations remain?

:::

## The Handoffs Matrix {#sec-nervous-handoffs-matrix}

When the mobile manipulator overruns a stop, the diagnosis starts by locating the fault at one of five canonical handoffs between the photons its cameras collect and the current its drives deliver. A cloud service governs its interfaces with service-level objectives (SLOs), such as a $P_{99}$ request latency, and when one is violated the runtime absorbs the error with retries, rerouting, or a degraded response. The five handoffs define **hard cyber-physical service-level objectives** instead. Software cannot recall momentum or undo heating in a winding, so no retry masks an unbudgeted interface violation.

Upstream, sensing transfers raw transducer signals to perception pipelines. Perception yields intermediate representations that fuse into an estimated world state. The state feeds the learned policy to produce an action plan. The plan submits candidate trajectories to the safety enforcer. Finally, the approved command passes from the enforcer to the physical actuators. Across each boundary, five interface limits govern feasibility: latency ($t_{\text{lat}}$), bandwidth ($\text{BW}$), energy and heat ($\mathcal{E}$), determinism ($\sigma_t$), and fault domain isolation ($\mathcal{F}$). The five handoffs and the five interface limits form a five-by-five matrix that maps every signal path to the physical budgets of the machine. The limits are distinct from the body's five budgets of @sec-body-five-budgets, which enter the matrix chiefly through its latency and energy columns. The record this section produces, the **handoff record**\index{Handoff record}, consumes the limit record of @sec-body-measuring-limits and the proposer limits established in @sec-brain, including latency, renewal frequency, and evidence age in the same structural format.

The example allocation in @tbl-04-synthesis-grid marks which limits are design-limiting at each handoff, and its numbers are chosen budgets, not measurements. The matrix gathers the budgets of all three Part I chapters, together with the sensor capture that @sec-boundary-machine-model places at the Boundary. In the Boundary row ($\mathcal{H}_1$), where the world becomes measurement, bandwidth and latency bind first, because raw multi-camera pixels stream over SerDes lanes and the exposure window sets a floor on image age before serialization begins. The Brain rows ($\mathcal{H}_2$, $\mathcal{H}_3$) bind first on energy and latency, the inference costs that @sec-brain established. The Body row ($\mathcal{H}_5$) binds first on determinism and heat, because the current loops of @sec-body must run on time and every ampere they deliver warms the windings and the power stage.

The Nervous System row ($\mathcal{H}_4$) is the architectural bridge that ties the Brain and the Body together. The proposal boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model) between the learned planner and the enforcer carries an action proposal ($p_t$), which consists of a compact spline parameterization or waypoint chunk. For the compact payload assumed in this grid, $\text{BW}< 100\text{ kB/s}$ is budgeted, so bandwidth does not bind at this boundary; latency, determinism ($\sigma_t$), and fault domain isolation ($\mathcal{F}$) do. The permission path isolates stochastic proposals with nonblocking mailboxes and expiring leases. On the mobile manipulator the latency limit is the chunk lease, which takes `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str` of the `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling_str` pre-brake ceiling at the drive limit (@sec-nervous-lease-sizing), and the active command is rechecked within each `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_tick_str` permission tick. Full trajectory admission has a separate work and response budget and must finish before a candidate becomes active; the tick does not imply that arbitrary map queries or whole-trajectory validation fit within it. Isolation rests on a private bus, a separate oscillator, and the isolated, held-up rail of @sec-nervous-hardware-isolation.

From the causal boundary perspective framed in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary, an interface failure can be localized to the handoff and budget it violates. Semantic mistakes or missing physical assumptions can still escape an otherwise timely interface; the matrix does not replace task evaluation or hazard analysis. When diagnosing an over-budget stop, trajectory overrun, or subsystem fault, engineers walk @tbl-04-synthesis-grid through a three-step operational root-cause procedure:

1. *Locate the boundary seam:* Identify which physical handoff ($\mathcal{H}_1\text{--}\mathcal{H}_5$) recorded the initial timing excursion, sequence gap, torn payload, or thermal trip.
2. *Check the binding dimension:* Query the specific physical limit ($t_{\text{lat}}, \text{BW}, \mathcal{E}, \sigma_t, \mathcal{F}$) designated as *BINDING* for that handoff cell, which dictates the resource bottleneck governing the interface.
3. *Evaluate like-for-like evidence:* Compare runtime diagnostic traces directly against the recorded bound kind (`requirement`, `proven bound`, or `measured distribution`), verifying whether the failure stemmed from an unmodeled microarchitectural tail event or a physical budget violation.

A handoff diagnosis must compare like evidence. For the $\mathcal{H}_2$ state-estimation path, suppose engineers allocate a $30.0\text{ ms}$ latency budget and measure $P_{99}=24.5\text{ ms}$ on a baseline hardware-in-the-loop run, a sampled margin of $+5.5\text{ ms}$. After thermal throttling, a measured $P_{99}=85.0\text{ ms}$ gives $-55.0\text{ ms}$ against that design budget. The decision is to reduce or reallocate workload and retain independent enforcement while revalidating. A $P_{99}$ sample diagnoses the regression; it is not a worst-case timing proof.

| Canonical Handoff Boundary                                  | Latency Limit ($t_{\text{lat}}$)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Bandwidth Limit ($\text{BW}$)                                                                                     | Energy & Heat Limit ($\mathcal{E}$)                                                                 | Determinism Limit ($\sigma_t$)                                                                     | Fault Domain Isolation ($\mathcal{F}$)                                                          |
|:------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **$\mathcal{H}_1$: Sensing $\to$ Perception** *(Boundary)*  | **BINDING** \newline $t_{\text{lat}} \le16.7\text{ ms}$, one frame period (sensor age dated at the frame's middle row; the oldest row is older, @sec-perception-observation-contract)                                                                                     | **BINDING** \newline $\text{BW}\ge 1.2\text{ GB/s}$ (multi-camera 4K uncompressed streams)                        | *Non-binding* \newline $P < 3\text{ W}$ (sensor head dissipation isolated)                          | **BINDING** \newline $\sigma_t \le 1.0\text{ ms}$ (frame-sync triggers prevent skew)               | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by SerDes hardware & DMA ring buffers                           |
| **$\mathcal{H}_2$: Perception $\to$ State** *(Brain)*       | **BINDING** \newline $t_{\text{lat}} \le30.0\text{ ms}$ (camera and inertial motion estimate & feature window)                                                                                                                                                                       | *Non-binding* \newline $\text{BW}\approx 10\text{--}50\text{ MB/s}$ (compressed image features & 3D occupancy cells)               | **BINDING** \newline $P \approx 15\text{--}35\text{ W}$ (edge vision backbone accelerator envelope) | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by sliding-window state estimator buffers                          | **BINDING** \newline Spatial memory isolation: MPUs prevent memory corruption                   |
| **$\mathcal{H}_3$: State $\to$ Plan** *(Brain)*             | **BINDING** \newline $t_{\text{lat}} \le100.0\text{ ms}$ (autoregressive tokenization & diffusion horizon)                                                                                                                                                                | *Non-binding* \newline $\text{BW}< 5\text{ MB/s}$ (low-dimensional state & prompt embeddings)                     | **BINDING** \newline $P \approx 30\text{--}75\text{ W}$ (transformer/diffusion matrix accelerators) | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by receding-horizon chunking & spline buffers                      | **BINDING** \newline Host faults must not halt the independent permission path                  |
| **$\mathcal{H}_4$: Plan $\to$ Enforcer** *(Nervous System)* | **BINDING** \newline chunk lease `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str` (candidate allocation; age at admission from @tbl-04-event-ledger); active-command checks within each `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_tick_str` tick; full admission budget recorded separately | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by compact parameterized splines ($\text{BW}< 100\text{ kB/s}$)                   | *Non-binding* \newline $P < 0.5\text{ W}$ (fixed-point constraint evaluation on MCU)                | **BINDING** \newline $\sigma_t \le 100\,\mu\text{s}$ (cycle-deterministic packet reception on MCU) | **BINDING** \newline Hardware boundary: private bus, separate oscillator, isolated held-up rail |
| **$\mathcal{H}_5$: Enforcer $\to$ Actuator** *(Body)*       | **BINDING** \newline $t_{\text{lat}} \le1.0\text{ ms}$ (servo interval $1.0\text{ ms}$; PWM loop $50\,\mu\text{s}$)                                                                                                                                                       | *Non-binding* \newline $\text{BW}\approx 1\text{--}5\text{ Mbps}$ (cyclic packets over deterministic command bus) | **BINDING** \newline $I^2 R$ copper winding dissipation, MOSFET switching losses                    | **BINDING** \newline $\sigma_t < 10\,\mu\text{s}$ (hard real-time PWM phase alignment & FOC)       | **BINDING** \newline Galvanic isolation, out-of-band analog E-stops, STO circuits               |

: **Handoffs-by-limits synthesis grid**: A five-by-five matrix mapping five canonical signal handoffs ($\mathcal{H}_1\text{--}\mathcal{H}_5$) across the Boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model), Brain (@sec-brain), Body (@sec-body), and Nervous System (@sec-nervous) against five physical limits ($t_{\text{lat}}, \text{BW}, \mathcal{E}, \sigma_t, \mathcal{F}$). Cells marked *BINDING* are the budgets that drive selection; *Non-binding* means the scenario budget meets that dimension with margin. These illustrative allocations organize the timing and isolation evidence still required; a non-binding cell is not a qualification verdict. {#tbl-04-synthesis-grid tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,18,16,16]"}

To ensure these budgets survive the lifecycle of the machine, every boundary condition in the grid is recorded as part of the machine's handoff record, the verifiable contract between hardware designers, systems engineers, and model developers. Each entry carries the six elements of a limit record (@sec-body-measuring-limits) and adds the fields that locate the limit at a handoff and say what kind of bound it is (@tbl-04-schema-notebook).

| Field Name               | Physical SI Units                                                | Structural Invariant & Description                                                                                                            |
|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `signal_id`              | dimensionless                                                    | Unique alphanumeric identifier (e.g. `SIG_VIO_01`, `SIG_TRQ_AX1`).                                                                            |
| `source_subsystem`       | dimensionless                                                    | Originating hardware or software module (`Camera_SerDes`, `Planner_VLA`).                                                                     |
| `destination_subsystem`  | dimensionless                                                    | Receiving hardware or software module (`State_Estimator`, `Safety_MCU`).                                                                      |
| `handoff`                | dimensionless                                                    | The handoff the signal crosses ($\mathcal{H}_1$ to $\mathcal{H}_5$).                                                                          |
| `physical_dimension`     | dimensionless                                                    | Target limit category ($t_{\text{lat}}$, $\text{BW}$, $\mathcal{E}$, $\sigma_t$, $\mathcal{F}$).                                              |
| `value`                  | SI units ($\text{ms}$, $\text{MB/s}$, $\text{W}$, $\mu\text{s}$) | Allocated budget, or the measured distribution it is checked against; for $\mathcal{H}_4$, the chunk lease derived from the stopping budget.  |
| `conditions`             | as recorded                                                      | Payload, temperature, supply voltage, firmware build, and concurrent workload under which the value holds; the value lapses when they change. |
| `uncertainty`            | same as `value`                                                  | Error bound of the instrument or model that produced the value.                                                                               |
| `margin`                 | same as `value`                                                  | Engineering margin between the operating target and the breakdown threshold.                                                                  |
| `detector`               | dimensionless                                                    | Runtime monitor that catches an excursion (for example, a lease timer, a rail-voltage monitor, or a phase-current sensor).                    |
| `provenance`             | dimensionless                                                    | Source of the value, including its evidence category (measured, derived, datasheet, or illustrative).                                         |
| `bound_kind`             | dimensionless                                                    | `requirement`, `proven bound`, or `measured distribution`; only a proven bound may stand in for a worst case.                                 |
| `clock_domain`           | dimensionless                                                    | Clock on which every time-valued field is expressed; a handoff that feeds the permission path uses the safety microcontroller's clock.        |
| `verification_timestamp` | UTC timestamp                                                    | Date of bench falsification and sign-off; a log field, never an input to an age test.                                                         |

: **Conceptual fields of the handoff record**: The six limit-record elements of @sec-body-measuring-limits, extended with the handoff, bound kind, and clock domain that locate a limit in the machine and state what evidence supports it. {#tbl-04-schema-notebook tbl-colwidths="[22,24,54]"}

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-event-ledger
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE CAPTURE-TO-BRAKE-ONSET EVENT LEDGER (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-04-event-ledger in @sec-nervous-handoffs-matrix; the ledger
# │          that @sec-body-latency-pipeline, @sec-perception-latency-waterfall,
# │          @sec-planning-horizon-tradeoff, and @sec-placement-isolation-decisions
# │          point to.
# │ Goal:    Name the four events once and show every interval between them from
# │          its one registry owner, so no chapter keeps its own stage list.
# │ Show:    capture -> dispatch 51.6 ms; dispatch -> admission 63.3 ms;
# │          L = 114.9 ms; admission -> brake onset 82 ms; capture -> brake
# │          onset 196.9 ms (= tau_delay 133.6 + Delta_da 63.3).
# │ How:     AISLE.perception_age, AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission,
# │          AISLE.t_capture_to_admission, AISLE.t_admission_to_brake_onset,
# │          AISLE.t_capture_to_brake_onset (MLSysIM).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class CaptureToBrakeLedger:
    """Three intervals between four events, each from its one registry owner."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)  # category: derived (capture to dispatch)
    t_da = AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission.to(millisecond)  # category: derived (allocation; dispatch to admission)
    t_resp = AISLE.t_admission_to_brake_onset.to(millisecond)  # category: derived (lease, tick, bus, onset)
    t_validate = AISLE.t_plan_validate.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative (inside t_da)
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay.to(millisecond)  # category: derived (the stopping ledger without t_da)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_replace = AISLE.t_capture_to_admission.to(millisecond)  # replacement latency L
    t_total = AISLE.t_capture_to_brake_onset.to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_age.magnitude - 51.6) < 1e-9, f"Capture-to-dispatch age drifted: {t_age}")
    check(abs(t_da.magnitude - 63.31072) < 1e-6, f"Dispatch-to-admission allocation drifted: {t_da}")
    check(abs((t_age + t_da - t_replace).magnitude) < 1e-9, "L must be the sum of the first two intervals.")
    check(abs(t_resp.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, f"Admission-to-onset response drifted: {t_resp}")
    check(abs((t_replace + t_resp - t_total).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The three intervals must close on the total.")
    check(abs((tau_delay + t_da - t_total).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The stopping ledger plus Delta_da must equal the total.")
    check(t_validate < t_da, "Validation is counted once, inside Delta_da.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_da_str = fmt_latency(t_da, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_replace_str = fmt_latency(t_replace, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_resp_str = fmt_latency(t_resp, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_total_str = fmt_latency(t_total, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

The latency column of the grid is read along one path, and the path needs one clock. Four **timing events**\index{Timing events!capture, dispatch, admission, brake onset} bound every interval on it. *Capture* is the exposure midpoint at which an observation is dated, inside $\mathcal{H}_1$. *Dispatch* is the moment perception publishes the dated record to the proposer, at $\mathcal{H}_2$. *Admission* is the moment the permission path accepts a chunk built on that record and starts its lease, at $\mathcal{H}_4$. *Brake onset* is the moment braking force begins, at $\mathcal{H}_5$. Between the four events lie three intervals, and each has one owner that derives it (@tbl-04-event-ledger). Every later chapter that charges time to this path uses these events and this ledger rather than a stage list of its own.

| Interval                                          | Opens at  | Closes at   | What it contains                                                                                                             |                                        Allocation | Derived in                         |
|:--------------------------------------------------|:----------|:------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------:|:-----------------------------------|
| **1.** Observation age $t_{\text{age}}$           | capture   | dispatch    | Half the exposure, readout, transport, DMA, image signal processing, perception backbone, hand-off to the proposer           |         `{python} CaptureToBrakeLedger.t_age_str` | @sec-perception-latency-waterfall  |
| **2.** Dispatch to admission $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ | dispatch  | admission   | Proposer inference (charged in full), board link, deserialization, whole-plan validation, activation, wait for the next tick |          `{python} CaptureToBrakeLedger.t_da_str` | @sec-placement-isolation-decisions |
| **1 + 2.** Replacement latency $L$                | capture   | admission   | Rows 1 and 2; validation is counted once, inside row 2                                                                       | **`{python} CaptureToBrakeLedger.t_replace_str`** | @sec-planning-horizon-tradeoff     |
| **3.** Stalled-proposer response                  | admission | brake onset | Chunk lease, one permission tick, one fieldbus cycle, brake onset                                                            |        `{python} CaptureToBrakeLedger.t_resp_str` | @sec-nervous-cadences              |
| **1 + 2 + 3.** Capture to brake onset             | capture   | brake onset | All three intervals                                                                                                          |   **`{python} CaptureToBrakeLedger.t_total_str`** | @sec-enforcement-composite-budget  |

: **The capture-to-brake-onset ledger of the running machine**: Four events bound three intervals, and each interval is derived in one chapter. Rows 1 and 3 together form the `{python} CaptureToBrakeLedger.tau_delay_str` pre-brake delay of the stopping budget; row 2 is the allocation that budget must still pay for. Row 2 charges the whole inference after dispatch, although its vision stage already lies in row 1, so the sum is conservative. Every value is an allocation or an illustrative stage time to qualify on the loaded machine, not a measurement. {#tbl-04-event-ledger tbl-colwidths="[20,9,9,34,12,16]"}

### Coupled budget synthesis for machine anatomy {#sec-nervous-coupled-budget}

The individual physical limits established across Part I do not operate in isolation: stopping distance, cognitive inference latency, memory bandwidth streaming, and deterministic command bus schedules converge into a single coupled timing inequality, the lease rule of @eq-nervous-lease-rule. By linking the distance budget of the Body with the compute throughput of the Brain, the Nervous System establishes the allowable operational envelope for the entire embodied machine.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-coupled-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PART I COUPLED BUDGET: DISTANCE -> LEASE -> SUPPLY -> LEASE RULE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-coupled-budget.
# │ Goal:    Join Ch2's distance terms, this chapter's lease, and Ch3's supply
# │          rates into the lease rule for the running machine.
# │ Show:    ceiling 258.3 ms; running total 835.5 mm; intent sweep 98.0 ms,
# │          intent 2 Hz / 336 ms computed (INT4 sweep 24.5 ms); chunk sweep
# │          1.12 ms, 20 Hz / 40 ms;
# │          50 + 5 = 55 ms < 60 ms lease; upper limit 236.3 ms, 184.7 ms
# │          after the 51.6 ms capture-to-dispatch age, 121.4 ms after the
# │          114.9 ms capture-to-admission age of @tbl-04-event-ledger
# │          (@eq-nervous-lease-rule).
# │ How:     ceiling and running total read from MachineLeaseBudget;
# │          calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization on RM / AISLE; the 5 ms renewal jitter is a scenario assumption.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PartOneCoupledBudget:
    """The chunk lease as the meeting point of Part I's distance, timing, and supply budgets."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    f_intent = RM.intent_rate  # category: chosen
    t_intent = RM.intent_inference_latency  # category: derived (prefill plus decode, @sec-brain-memory-wall)
    f_chunk = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    t_chunk = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative (P99, incl. vision)
    t_renewal_jitter = MachineLeaseBudget.t_renewal_jitter  # category: chosen (from calc-nervous-machine-lease-budget)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_ceiling = MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling  # from calc-nervous-machine-lease-budget
    running_total = MachineLeaseBudget.running_total  # one source for the stopping budget

    intent_sweep = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=RM.intent_weight_memory,  # deployed INT4 weights
        memory_bandwidth=RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth,
        chunk_horizon=RM.chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=RM.dram_efficiency,
    )["t_stream"].to(millisecond)
    chunk_sweep = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=memory_from_params(RM.chunk_model.parameters, BYTES_FP16 / param),
        memory_bandwidth=RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth,
        chunk_horizon=RM.chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=RM.dram_efficiency,
    )["t_stream"].to(millisecond)

    t_chunk_period = (1 / f_chunk).to(millisecond)
    t_renewal_need = (t_chunk_period + t_renewal_jitter).to(millisecond)  # lease lower limit
    t_lease_upper = (t_ceiling - t_tick - t_bus - t_act).to(millisecond)  # before observation age
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)  # capture-to-dispatch age only (@sec-perception)
    t_lease_upper_age = (t_lease_upper - t_age).to(millisecond)  # before the dispatch-to-admission allocation
    t_age_admit = CaptureToBrakeLedger.t_replace  # capture to admission, rows 1 + 2 of @tbl-04-event-ledger
    t_lease_upper_admit = (t_lease_upper - t_age_admit).to(millisecond)  # with Delta_da allocated
    mm_per_ms = (v * (1 * millisecond)).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_ceiling.magnitude - 258.333) < 5e-3, f"Pre-brake ceiling drifted: {t_ceiling}")
    check(abs(running_total.magnitude - 835.5) < 1e-6, f"Running total drifted: {running_total}")
    # 2026-09-28 (M2): deployed INT4 intent weights; ACT corrected to about 80M parameters.
    check(abs(intent_sweep.magnitude - 24.51) < 5e-3, f"Intent weight sweep drifted: {intent_sweep}")
    check(abs(chunk_sweep.magnitude - 1.1204) < 5e-4, f"Chunk weight sweep drifted: {chunk_sweep}")
    check(abs(f_chunk.to(hertz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk rate drifted: {f_chunk}")
    check(abs(f_intent.to(hertz).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Intent rate drifted: {f_intent}")
    check(abs(t_chunk.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk inference latency drifted: {t_chunk}")
    check(abs(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude - 335.61) < 5e-3, f"Intent inference latency drifted: {t_intent}")
    check(abs(t_chunk_period.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-6, f"Chunk period drifted: {t_chunk_period}")
    check(t_intent > t_lease, "The intent model must be unable to renew a chunk lease")
    check(t_chunk < t_chunk_period, "Chunk inference must finish within the chunk period")
    check(abs(t_renewal_need.magnitude - 55.0) < 1e-6, f"Lease lower limit drifted: {t_renewal_need}")
    check(t_renewal_need < t_lease, "Lease rule: chunk period plus jitter must be shorter than the lease")
    check(abs(t_lease_upper.magnitude - 236.333) < 5e-3, f"Lease upper limit (before age) drifted: {t_lease_upper}")
    check(t_lease <= t_lease_upper - AISLE.perception_age, "Lease rule: lease must fit the ceiling after tick, bus, onset, and age")
    check(abs(t_age.magnitude - 51.6) < 1e-6, f"Capture-to-dispatch age drifted: {t_age}")
    # margin_lease_rule_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 55, 60, and 184.7 ms.
    check(abs(t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Lease drifted: {t_lease}")
    check(abs(t_lease_upper_age.magnitude - 184.733) < 5e-3, f"Lease upper limit after age drifted: {t_lease_upper_age}")
    check(abs(t_lease_upper_admit.magnitude - 121.423) < 5e-3, f"Lease upper limit at admission drifted: {t_lease_upper_admit}")
    check(t_lease < t_lease_upper_admit, "Lease rule: the lease must still fit once Delta_da is allocated")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    t_ceiling_str = fmt_latency(t_ceiling, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    running_total_str = fmt_length(running_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    intent_sweep_str = fmt_latency(intent_sweep, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_intent_str = fmt_latency(round(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_intent_str = fmt_frequency(f_intent, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    chunk_sweep_str = fmt_latency(chunk_sweep, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    f_chunk_str = fmt_frequency(f_chunk, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    t_chunk_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_jitter_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_jitter, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_need_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_need, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_upper_str = fmt_latency(t_lease_upper, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_lease_upper_age_str = fmt_latency(t_lease_upper_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_age_admit_str = fmt_latency(t_age_admit, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_lease_upper_admit_str = fmt_latency(t_lease_upper_admit, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    mm_per_ms_str = fmt_length(mm_per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

The three chapters of Part I each set terms of one budget, and the chunk lease is where they meet. @Sec-body-kinetic-momentum fixed the distance side. At its `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.v_str` drive limit the loaded machine must stop inside the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.d_clear_str` clear distance at a rack end, and the braking term and the fixed overheads leave `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_ceiling_str` for everything that happens before braking force begins. @Sec-nervous-cadences spent part of that time. A proposer that stalls keeps its authority for one lease, the stop reaches the drives one tick and one bus cycle later, and the stopping budget stands at `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.running_total_str`.

The lease cannot be made as short as the budget would like, because a proposer must renew it. @Sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline established what each learned proposer can supply. The intent model's INT4 weights take `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.intent_sweep_str` to stream from memory once, but a full inference, a compute-bound prefill followed by bandwidth-bound decode sweeps, takes `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_intent_str`, so at `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.f_intent_str` it cannot renew a proposal every few tens of milliseconds. The chunk policy's weights stream in `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.chunk_sweep_str`, and its selected `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.f_chunk_str` cadence calls for a fresh chunk every `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_chunk_period_str`. Its illustrative `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_chunk_str` P99 inference time makes that cadence a plausible supply target, not a guaranteed renewal bound. Late or missing renewals remain the permission path's responsibility.

::: {.column-margin}
<!-- fig-alt hand-types 55, 60, and 184.7 ms; PartOneCoupledBudget guards them.
     Drawn by generate_margin_figures.py (ch04_lease_rule_envelope); --check fails on drift. -->
![](images/svg/margin_lease_rule_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars in milliseconds against a dashed red ceiling at 184.7 milliseconds: renewal floor 55 milliseconds and lease 60 milliseconds, both far to the left of the ceiling."}

*The lease must outlast renewal and expire well before the stopping budget runs out.*
:::

These facts fix the **lease rule**\index{Chunk lease!lease rule} for this machine. For continuous tracking, the lease must outlast the chosen successful-admission interval plus its variation allowance. It must also fit inside the pre-brake ceiling of @eq-nervous-prebrake once detection, transport, brake onset, and the evidence age at admission are reserved:
$$T_{\text{chunk}} + T_{\text{jitter}} < T_{\text{lease}} \le \frac{D_{\text{clear}} - \delta_{\text{loc}} - \delta_{\text{margin}} - v^2/2a_{\text{brake}}}{v} - T_{\text{tick}} - T_{\text{bus}} - T_{\text{act}} - t_{\text{age}}$$ {#eq-nervous-lease-rule}
where $T_{\text{chunk}}$ is the chunk policy's renewal period and $T_{\text{jitter}}$ the allowance for its variation between successful admissions. The inequality is the coupled budget of Part I in one line. Its left side is supply, set by the proposer of @sec-brain. Its first term on the right is distance, set by the speed, the clearance, and the brake of @sec-body. The remaining terms are this chapter's detection and transport delays, the body's brake onset, and the evidence age that @sec-perception accounts for. A faster machine, a weaker brake, or a shorter clearance lowers the right side; a slower proposer raises the left; and the design has no admissible lease once the two sides cross. On the mobile manipulator the left side is the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_renewal_need_str` floor of \ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}. The right side is `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_upper_str` before evidence age, and subtracting the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_age_str` capture-to-dispatch age developed in @sec-perception leaves `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_upper_age_str`. The evidence age at admission is longer, because the record still has to cross dispatch to admission. Charging that interval's allocation from @tbl-04-event-ledger makes the age at admission `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_age_admit_str` and leaves `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_upper_admit_str`. The chosen `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_str` sits just above the renewal target, because every millisecond of lease costs `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.mm_per_ms_str` at the drive limit. It remains a candidate allocation until the loaded machine measures the ledger's intervals and they fit. Increasing the lease to hide admission delays would spend further clearance rather than close that budget.

Each chunk carries the base's velocity and the arm's joint targets together, so the selected architecture uses one candidate lease for both bodies. Each body must have a feasible state-matched response when that lease lapses. The base's `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_ceiling_str` pre-brake ceiling constrains the allocation here; it does not establish that the arm has more margin. The illustrative arm calculation in @sec-planning-handoff checks response travel and stopping against its own clearance. Qualifying the shared lease requires both bodies' timing, evidence, current state, and fallback limits to hold. The arm's evidence horizon bounds a different lease, the intent lease, which limits how long an admitted goal from the intent model stays valid, and the intent model's slower targets expire under it (@sec-intent-lease).

The $\mathcal{H}_4$ row of @tbl-04-synthesis-grid is this chapter's handoff record filled in, combining the limit record (@sec-body) with the proposer limits from @sec-brain. Its value is the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_str` chunk lease handed from the chunk policy to the permission path, a `requirement` proposed for the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.v_str` drive limit, loaded, on a dry floor, at the admission-renewal target above; its final margin remains unresolved until the allocated intervals of @tbl-04-event-ledger and the remaining stop terms are measured, and its detector is the lease timer on the safety microcontroller, counted on that processor's own clock.

::: {#chk-nervous-handoffs-grid .callout-checkpoint title="The handoffs matrix and physical budgets"}
